extraction.body: A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations was caused by an issue following a copper wire upgrade, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said. Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem was caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades, or faulty equipment. The US government does not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack, although an investigation is still under way, Duffy said. Friday's suspension was the longest such incident since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US and the disruption is expected to last for days. Maintenance was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider company, Duffy said. The US has "an incredibly old telecommunications system", he added. "It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued," he said. The transport secretary explained that a router that was being worked on had started flooding other air traffic control systems and created communication issues with planes which led the government to shut down the airspace for safety reasons. Bryan Bedford, who heads the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), told the same news conference: "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI related." On Saturday L3Harris said it had completed over 70% of the work to modernise communications infrastructure before the shutdown. "We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel," it said in a statement. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously." No flights were allowed to take off from the continental US for more than four hours from 15:54 EST (19:54 GMT) on Friday. More than 3,500 flights were cancelled and more than 2,000 delayed in the US on Saturday, according to tracking website Flight Aware, as knock-on disruption continues. In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to the gates. Some international flights were allowed to depart US airports, in an apparent effort to clear space. Duffy warned that a similar issue could arise again unless the US Congress approved upgrades to air traffic control infrastructure. US President Donald Trump has requested $30.1bn for the upgrades. Both chambers of Congress are currently controlled by the Republican Party. Former TSA Administrator John Pistole told the BBC that "the fact that they were able to get it restarted in four-and-a-half hours is good news - it shows a resilience in the system - but what's to say it's not going to happen tomorrow?" A nationwide ground stop has only been ordered one other time since all flights were banned from take-off for several days following the 11 September 2001 attacks. It is the latest development in a months-long challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links.

extraction.body: At a press conference today, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that Friday’s nationwide ground stop ordered by the FAA was related to work replacing outdated copper wire with a fiber optic line at a “remote FAA facility.” The secretary said that this was “routine maintenance,” rather than the result of a major modernization effort. He told reporters that it was “such an old wire that it was being discontinued, meaning that line was going to get shut down,” necessitating the upgrade. What wasn’t clear, according to Secretary Duffy, was the root cause of the problem. He said that it could have been faulty hardware, a misconfigured router, or “incompetence” on the part of contractor L3Harris. Regardless, what followed was the newly installed router “flooding” other routers in the Air Traffic Control system. “We are building, we are building safely, but we are building fast,” he said, but said that Congress had only given him a “partial payment” to complete the necessary work. In a statement posted to their site, L3Harris said: > L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA. With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator (FAA) Bryan Bedford provided updates on what led to the FAA’s nationwide ground stop on November 13, 2026, and the restoration efforts the Department took to reopen the airspace safely and quickly. REMINDER: Telecommunications issues that impacted the stability of communications and radar systems utilized by Air Traffic Control led the FAA to issue a nationwide ground stop out of an abundance of caution. FAA’s incredible air traffic controllers and commercial pilots were responsible for safely and efficiently grounding over 3,500 flights swiftly. Once the ground stop lifted, over 8,000 flight operations resumed last night alone. Today, the airspace is open, however, passengers should be prepared for some delays and cancellations as flights resume. Secretary Duffy on the work done by air traffic controllers and pilots to land Americans safely yesterday: “I just want to, again, start off and thank our air traffic controllers and our pilots. They exhibited an amazing performance yesterday. We had 3,500 aircraft in the air. We had a ground stop and they safely landed all of our aircraft which was outstanding. But I also want to thank our flight attendants, our ground crews, our airport authorities. All of them rallied yesterday. A lot of passengers at airports. They all came together and served the American people incredibly well. I also want to thank the passengers. I know a lot of people were disrupted. Whether they were going on vacation, they were coming home from work–they had significant disruption and the patience that they exhibited. We at the DOT and the FAA are grateful for that patience.” Secretary Duffy on what led to the issue: “Now, those of you who are aviation reporters have heard me talk about a decades old air traffic control system. It's not just old equipment. We have an incredibly old telecommunication system. And so, here's what we believe happened yesterday: Secretary Duffy on whether the inconsistencies were caused by a cyber attack: “We don't believe so. Once we were able to isolate the work that was being done at this remote location, all of our systems came back online. So, we don't believe this was cyber at all.” Secretary Duffy on the safety of the national airspace: “To the American traveler, our number one job is their safety and Bryan [Bedford] mentioned this and I’ve mentioned this before but we will keep you on the ground, you won’t get to your destination if we think you can’t get there safely. My first day on the job was the DCA air crash…My heart goes out to those families and everyone who has lost someone in aviation. We do everything we can to keep travelers safe and our airspace is safe. I fly all the time, my kids fly, my wife flies. This is a safe system, evidenced by what happened yesterday. If there is any issue with our telecom…we shut the airspace down. We brought airplanes in, we landed them safely, we figured out what was wrong, our systems came back online and have become fully operational. That’s how seriously we take safety. ” Secretary Duffy on the FAA’s progress modernizing America’s air traffic control system: “The Congress gave me a partial payment. They gave me $12.5 billion. And one of the problems that we had was [Congress] weren't quite sure that we would spend the money well and we'd build with the money. And that's the history of the FAA that goes back from Republicans and Democrats. They haven't spent the money well. So, they want to make sure we're going to spend and spend it well. And we have. And so, in the course of the last year, since I've got that $12.5 billion, I want to talk to you about what we've actually accomplished. Secretary Duffy on the need for Congress to fully fund air traffic control modernization: “I hope that they meet this moment and they invest in what will be the state-of-the-art, the best-in-class, best in the world air traffic control system. When I came in, President Trump, before the DCA air crash, was saying, ‘We have to modernize our airspace. I want you to work on modernizing air traffic control.’...and then if you look at the Congress–that you have both Democrats and Republicans who understand how important this is. For me, it gets to be frustrating where everyone says they want to do it and the president is pushing it but we don't get the resources. And I think this is the moment. If we don't start to switch out our systems, how long are we going to wait? I think this is a sign for [Congress] to lean in. This is bipartisan….We should be able to rely on our air traffic control system—making sure it works… Let’s not let the legacy of the past where investments weren't made, which is why we are here today. Let's make the investments and look forward to a brighter future in aviation , a safer future, a more efficient future in aviation.” FAA Administrator Bedford on how the issue is unrelated to USDOT’s ongoing modernization efforts: “I think we’re conflating ‘Modernization’ with this upgrade at this particular facility. We spend a billion dollars a year maintaining and sustaining the existing 1980’s TDMI telco network—call it 1G, the 1G system that the FAA is on. So we are constantly replacing 2,000 Cisco 600 routers with Juniper routers. So, this is ordinary course-of-business stuff, this is not part of the Peraton-FAA $12.5 billion modernization effort, so let’s not conflate those two things.” Secretary Duffy on the timing of the upgrade: “We're making the transition because it's safer and it's more resilient. But because of the nature of what this switchover was, it was a remote location, we'll do those during the day. Now, if we're going to be at Newark, if we're going to be, you know, in one of our big facilities, those switchovers happen at night and they can have a bigger impact. But these smaller locations don't have that kind of impact—or they shouldn't have that kind of impact which is what we saw yesterday. So, there'll be a reevaluation of when we do this work. But when you look across the country when the work has been done from copper to fiber, going from analog to digital, they've happened at all times of the day, and so we have to drill in a little further about what happened here.”

extraction.body: Airlines canceled thousands of flights across the U.S. on Saturday as they worked to recover from a nationwide ground stop a day earlier that left passengers scrambling for seats and disrupted travel around the world. The U.S. air travel schedule should be back to normal by the end of Sunday, two days after what was the nation's longest ground stop in 25 years, Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters in Washington on Saturday. He said airlines "will still have delays and cancellations" Saturday but promised that the "worst is behind us." Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the problem began when contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. was replacing a section of the air traffic control system's old copper wire with new fiber wire, somehow causing the system to overload. The work led to "intermittent" communications and radar gaps, prompting the government to shut down air traffic for more than four hours. WATCH: FAA issues rare nationwide ground stop due to 'extraordinary circumstances' Duffy said officials were investigating whether contractor "incompetence" or a faulty router was the cause. "Our contractor didn't meet the moment or the equipment didn't meet the moment," he added. L3Harris said it was supporting the FAA in its investigation to "understand the conditions" that led to the ground stop. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," it said in a statement. The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said Friday's stoppage affected about a quarter of the 45,000 flights in the U.S. each day. "The knock-on effect of that is incredible," said Charlton, managing director of Aviation Advocacy. "The aircraft doesn't just fly from A to B and back … and then stop. It then moves onto C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you're talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific." At airports across the U.S. on Saturday, passengers were still scrambling to figure out how to get to their destinations. Some waited out the chaos in hotels, others sprinted to snag rental cars and bus or train tickets. Many were forced to camp out in airports. Others got creative. Video in Seattle's airport showed a passenger serenading stressed out travelers with classical music. Stranded strangers participated in a cornhole tournament at the Lexington, Kentucky, airport. The singer T-Pain and the band Hoobastank were captured on video singing to passengers as they waited on commercial airplanes. extraction.body: A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations was caused by an issue following a copper wire upgrade, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said. Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem was caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades, or faulty equipment. The US government does not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack, although an investigation is still under way, Duffy said. Friday's suspension was the longest such incident since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US and the disruption is expected to last for days. Maintenance was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider company, Duffy said. The US has "an incredibly old telecommunications system", he added. "It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued," he said. The transport secretary explained that a router that was being worked on had started flooding other air traffic control systems and created communication issues with planes which led the government to shut down the airspace for safety reasons. Bryan Bedford, who heads the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), told the same news conference: "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI related." On Saturday L3Harris said it had completed over 70% of the work to modernise communications infrastructure before the shutdown. "We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel," it said in a statement. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously." No flights were allowed to take off from the continental US for more than four hours from 15:54 EST (19:54 GMT) on Friday. More than 3,500 flights were cancelled and more than 2,000 delayed in the US on Saturday, according to tracking website Flight Aware, as knock-on disruption continues. In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to the gates. Some international flights were allowed to depart US airports, in an apparent effort to clear space. Duffy warned that a similar issue could arise again unless the US Congress approved upgrades to air traffic control infrastructure. US President Donald Trump has requested $30.1bn for the upgrades. Both chambers of Congress are currently controlled by the Republican Party. Former TSA Administrator John Pistole told the BBC that "the fact that they were able to get it restarted in four-and-a-half hours is good news - it shows a resilience in the system - but what's to say it's not going to happen tomorrow?" A nationwide ground stop has only been ordered one other time since all flights were banned from take-off for several days following the 11 September 2001 attacks. WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator (FAA) Bryan Bedford provided updates on what led to the FAA’s nationwide ground stop on November 13, 2026, and the restoration efforts the Department took to reopen the airspace safely and quickly. REMINDER: Telecommunications issues that impacted the stability of communications and radar systems utilized by Air Traffic Control led the FAA to issue a nationwide ground stop out of an abundance of caution. FAA’s incredible air traffic controllers and commercial pilots were responsible for safely and efficiently grounding over 3,500 flights swiftly. Once the ground stop lifted, over 8,000 flight operations resumed last night alone. Today, the airspace is open, however, passengers should be prepared for some delays and cancellations as flights resume. Secretary Duffy on the work done by air traffic controllers and pilots to land Americans safely yesterday: “I just want to, again, start off and thank our air traffic controllers and our pilots. They exhibited an amazing performance yesterday. We had 3,500 aircraft in the air. We had a ground stop and they safely landed all of our aircraft which was outstanding. But I also want to thank our flight attendants, our ground crews, our airport authorities. All of them rallied yesterday. A lot of passengers at airports. They all came together and served the American people incredibly well. I also want to thank the passengers. I know a lot of people were disrupted. Whether they were going on vacation, they were coming home from work–they had significant disruption and the patience that they exhibited. We at the DOT and the FAA are grateful for that patience.” Secretary Duffy on what led to the issue: “Now, those of you who are aviation reporters have heard me talk about a decades old air traffic control system. It's not just old equipment. We have an incredibly old telecommunication system. And so, here's what we believe happened yesterday: Secretary Duffy on whether the inconsistencies were caused by a cyber attack: “We don't believe so. Once we were able to isolate the work that was being done at this remote location, all of our systems came back online. So, we don't believe this was cyber at all.” Secretary Duffy on the safety of the national airspace: “To the American traveler, our number one job is their safety and Bryan [Bedford] mentioned this and I’ve mentioned this before but we will keep you on the ground, you won’t get to your destination if we think you can’t get there safely. My first day on the job was the DCA air crash…My heart goes out to those families and everyone who has lost someone in aviation. We do everything we can to keep travelers safe and our airspace is safe. I fly all the time, my kids fly, my wife flies. This is a safe system, evidenced by what happened yesterday. If there is any issue with our telecom…we shut the airspace down. We brought airplanes in, we landed them safely, we figured out what was wrong, our systems came back online and have become fully operational. That’s how seriously we take safety. ” Secretary Duffy on the FAA’s progress modernizing America’s air traffic control system: “The Congress gave me a partial payment. They gave me $12.5 billion. And one of the problems that we had was [Congress] weren't quite sure that we would spend the money well and we'd build with the money. And that's the history of the FAA that goes back from Republicans and Democrats. They haven't spent the money well. So, they want to make sure we're going to spend and spend it well. And we have. And so, in the course of the last year, since I've got that $12.5 billion, I want to talk to you about what we've actually accomplished. Secretary Duffy on the need for Congress to fully fund air traffic control modernization: “I hope that they meet this moment and they invest in what will be the state-of-the-art, the best-in-class, best in the world air traffic control system. When I came in, President Trump, before the DCA air crash, was saying, ‘We have to modernize our airspace. I want you to work on modernizing air traffic control.’...and then if you look at the Congress–that you have both Democrats and Republicans who understand how important this is. For me, it gets to be frustrating where everyone says they want to do it and the president is pushing it but we don't get the resources. And I think this is the moment. If we don't start to switch out our systems, how long are we going to wait? I think this is a sign for [Congress] to lean in. This is bipartisan….We should be able to rely on our air traffic control system—making sure it works… Let’s not let the legacy of the past where investments weren't made, which is why we are here today. Let's make the investments and look forward to a brighter future in aviation , a safer future, a more efficient future in aviation.” FAA Administrator Bedford on how the issue is unrelated to USDOT’s ongoing modernization efforts: “I think we’re conflating ‘Modernization’ with this upgrade at this particular facility. We spend a billion dollars a year maintaining and sustaining the existing 1980’s TDMI telco network—call it 1G, the 1G system that the FAA is on. So we are constantly replacing 2,000 Cisco 600 routers with Juniper routers. So, this is ordinary course-of-business stuff, this is not part of the Peraton-FAA $12.5 billion modernization effort, so let’s not conflate those two things.” Secretary Duffy on the timing of the upgrade: “We're making the transition because it's safer and it's more resilient. But because of the nature of what this switchover was, it was a remote location, we'll do those during the day. Now, if we're going to be at Newark, if we're going to be, you know, in one of our big facilities, those switchovers happen at night and they can have a bigger impact. But these smaller locations don't have that kind of impact—or they shouldn't have that kind of impact which is what we saw yesterday. So, there'll be a reevaluation of when we do this work. But when you look across the country when the work has been done from copper to fiber, going from analog to digital, they've happened at all times of the day, and so we have to drill in a little further about what happened here.”

extraction.body: Airlines canceled thousands of flights across the U.S. on Saturday as they worked to recover from a nationwide ground stop a day earlier that left passengers scrambling for seats and disrupted travel around the world. The U.S. air travel schedule should be back to normal by the end of Sunday, two days after what was the nation's longest ground stop in 25 years, Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters in Washington on Saturday. He said airlines "will still have delays and cancellations" Saturday but promised that the "worst is behind us." Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the problem began when contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. was replacing a section of the air traffic control system's old copper wire with new fiber wire, somehow causing the system to overload. The work led to "intermittent" communications and radar gaps, prompting the government to shut down air traffic for more than four hours. WATCH: FAA issues rare nationwide ground stop due to 'extraordinary circumstances' Duffy said officials were investigating whether contractor "incompetence" or a faulty router was the cause. "Our contractor didn't meet the moment or the equipment didn't meet the moment," he added. L3Harris said it was supporting the FAA in its investigation to "understand the conditions" that led to the ground stop. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," it said in a statement. The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said Friday's stoppage affected about a quarter of the 45,000 flights in the U.S. each day. "The knock-on effect of that is incredible," said Charlton, managing director of Aviation Advocacy. "The aircraft doesn't just fly from A to B and back … and then stop. It then moves onto C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you're talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific." At airports across the U.S. on Saturday, passengers were still scrambling to figure out how to get to their destinations. Some waited out the chaos in hotels, others sprinted to snag rental cars and bus or train tickets. Many were forced to camp out in airports. Others got creative. Video in Seattle's airport showed a passenger serenading stressed out travelers with classical music. Stranded strangers participated in a cornhole tournament at the Lexington, Kentucky, airport. The singer T-Pain and the band Hoobastank were captured on video singing to passengers as they waited on commercial airplanes. Dan Russell, 66, learned his connecting flight from Kona, Hawaii, to Fresno, California, was canceled a half-hour before boarding was scheduled in San Diego on Friday night. Hotels were full, so he and his wife waited at the airport for a rebooked flight. "There's nothing you can do," Russell said, as his wife, Mary, tried to nap on his shoulder. WATCH: Homeland Security Secretary Mullin says FAA flight stoppage 'isn't another 9/11' A cheerful Southwest Airlines gate agent at Dallas Love Field greeted passengers at dawn with, "Good morning, good morning," then repeatedly said all flights were full and asked passengers to have boarding passes ready to help keep flights moving. In Las Vegas, Korean Mexican influencer Sujin Kim, known online as Chingu Amiga, said her flight to Mexico was rescheduled for Saturday morning. "Many people ended up sleeping at the airport, too, but thank God we managed to find a room," she said. At the Newark, New Jersey, airport, Umi Egchi was trying to figure out when his flights would line up so he could return home to Japan. "I'm not sure exactly what happened. I just want to go home," said Egchi, who had a sleep mask on top of his head. Sports teams that traveled for games this weekend adjusted game start times, and No. 19 Mississippi's game at Oklahoma was delayed a full day to Sunday. FlightAware, a website that tracks flights, said more than 5,100 flights within, into or out of the U.S. had been canceled Saturday. Duffy reiterated Saturday that no one was in danger as more than 3,000 flights in the air at the time of the grounding order landed safely. Trump administration officials also blamed Congress for failing to approve more funding to replace the decades-old technology that helps manage the U.S. air traffic. Duffy said that 70% of the system had been replaced with fiber optic wire but that his agency also needs new air traffic control towers and runways. The FAA has replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of an overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work. "We have aging infrastructure throughout the airspace," Duffy said, while stressing that flying remains safe. "You won't get to your destination if we don't think you can get there safely." In a moment that perhaps only further underscored the Transportation Department's struggling systems, Duffy's news conference Saturday morning began with audio troubles that forced last-minute microphone swaps. Although Duffy said he had repeatedly spoken with President Donald Trump since the ground stop began, the president has largely been quiet on the topic. He has not spoken publicly on the matter, nor issued statements via social media, although he commented on other things. He spoke on the phone with a Fox News reporter, but that was not on camera. Charlton, the aviation consultant, pointed to the difficulties of updating a system that can never shut down. Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference Friday was the nationwide scale of the disruption, which left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots. "If you don't have that ability, whether it's because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you've got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you're going to risk not being able to communicate with them," said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot. Kruesi reported from Providence, Rhode Island. Associated Press journalists Jill Colvin in New York, Seung Min Kim in Washington, Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, Elliot Spagat in San Diego, Bernice Bautista in Las Vegas, Marc Levy in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania and Hannah Fingerhut in Des Moines, Iowa, also contributed. The U.S. air travel schedule should be back to normal by the end of Sunday, two days after what was the nation's longest ground stop in 25 years, Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters in Washington on Saturday. He said airlines "will still have delays and cancellations" Saturday but promised that the "worst is behind us."

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the problem began when contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. was replacing a section of the air traffic control system's old copper wire with new fiber wire, somehow causing the system to overload. The work led to "intermittent" communications and radar gaps, prompting the government to shut down air traffic for more than four hours.
WATCH: FAA issues rare nationwide ground stop due to 'extraordinary circumstances'
Duffy said officials were investigating whether contractor "incompetence" or a faulty router was the cause. "Our contractor didn't meet the moment or the equipment didn't meet the moment," he added.
L3Harris said it was supporting the FAA in its investigation to "understand the conditions" that led to the ground stop.
"L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," it said in a statement.
The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said Friday's stoppage affected about a quarter of the 45,000 flights in the U.S. each day.

"The knock-on effect of that is incredible," said Charlton, managing director of Aviation Advocacy. "The aircraft doesn't just fly from A to B and back … and then stop. It then moves onto C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you're talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific."

At airports across the U.S. on Saturday, passengers were still scrambling to figure out how to get to their destinations. Some waited out the chaos in hotels, others sprinted to snag rental cars and bus or train tickets. Many were forced to camp out in airports.

Others got creative. Video in Seattle's airport showed a passenger serenading stressed out travelers with classical music. Stranded strangers participated in a cornhole tournament at the Lexington, Kentucky, airport. The singer T-Pain and the band Hoobastank were captured on video singing to passengers as they waited on commercial airplanes.

Dan Russell, 66, learned his connecting flight from Kona, Hawaii, to Fresno, California, was canceled a half-hour before boarding was scheduled in San Diego on Friday night. Hotels were full, so he and his wife waited at the airport for a rebooked flight.
"There's nothing you can do," Russell said, as his wife, Mary, tried to nap on his shoulder.
WATCH: Homeland Security Secretary Mullin says FAA flight stoppage 'isn't another 9/11'

A cheerful Southwest Airlines gate agent at Dallas Love Field greeted passengers at dawn with, "Good morning, good morning," then repeatedly said all flights were full and asked passengers to have boarding passes ready to help keep flights moving.

In Las Vegas, Korean Mexican influencer Sujin Kim, known online as Chingu Amiga, said her flight to Mexico was rescheduled for Saturday morning. "Many people ended up sleeping at the airport, too, but thank God we managed to find a room," she said.
At the Newark, New Jersey, airport, Umi Egchi was trying to figure out when his flights would line up so he could return home to Japan.
"I'm not sure exactly what happened. I just want to go home," said Egchi, who had a sleep mask on top of his head.
Sports teams that traveled for games this weekend adjusted game start times, and No. 19 Mississippi's game at Oklahoma was delayed a full day to Sunday.
FlightAware, a website that tracks flights, said more than 5,100 flights within, into or out of the U.S. had been canceled Saturday.
Duffy reiterated Saturday that no one was in danger as more than 3,000 flights in the air at the time of the grounding order landed safely.

Trump administration officials also blamed Congress for failing to approve more funding to replace the decades-old technology that helps manage the U.S. air traffic. Duffy said that 70% of the system had been replaced with fiber optic wire but that his agency also needs new air traffic control towers and runways.

The FAA has replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of an overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
"We have aging infrastructure throughout the airspace," Duffy said, while stressing that flying remains safe. "You won't get to your destination if we don't think you can get there safely."

In a moment that perhaps only further underscored the Transportation Department's struggling systems, Duffy's news conference Saturday morning began with audio troubles that forced last-minute microphone swaps.

Although Duffy said he had repeatedly spoken with President Donald Trump since the ground stop began, the president has largely been quiet on the topic. He has not spoken publicly on the matter, nor issued statements via social media, although he commented on other things. He spoke on the phone with a Fox News reporter, but that was not on camera.
Charlton, the aviation consultant, pointed to the difficulties of updating a system that can never shut down.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference Friday was the nationwide scale of the disruption, which left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.

"If you don't have that ability, whether it's because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you've got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you're going to risk not being able to communicate with them," said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.

Kruesi reported from Providence, Rhode Island. Associated Press journalists Jill Colvin in New York, Seung Min Kim in Washington, Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, Elliot Spagat in San Diego, Bernice Bautista in Las Vegas, Marc Levy in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania and Hannah Fingerhut in Des Moines, Iowa, also contributed.
Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.

passages: This article originally appeared on Moneywise.com under the title: Elon Musk joins 100,000+ signers on a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang — including 5,000+ who say they work at Nvidia
In an informal poll, we asked Moneywise followers whether Nvidia should bring Jensen back.
Of 164 votes, 82% said "most definitely." Just 6% said "absolutely not," while 12% picked "he's poaching them all," a nod to the idea that Nvidia employees would follow Huang wherever he goes next.
The site says it isn't affiliated with Nvidia or Huang.
Signers identify themselves, and organizers say they may hold new signatures for review before counting them.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Huang co-founded the chipmaker in 1993 and led it for 33 years, building it into one of the world's most valuable companies.
12 that he had resigned as president, CEO and board member , effective immediately.
CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO , and director Harvey Jones became the board's first-ever chair.
When Ravikant followed up by calling Huang "the Steve Jobs of Nvidia" and "irreplaceable," Musk replied "True." He also replied "Always" to a post praising him for being a true friend to Huang.
Musk also has a business stake in the outcome.
His rocket and AI company, SpaceX [NASDAQ: SPCX], has committed to building its AI data centers exclusively with Nvidia chips, and Nvidia owns a stake in SpaceX worth billions .
The petition site also lists him as an Nvidia shareholder.

His exit came after reports that he'd had extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspect was recruited by China's top spy agency.
Neither he nor Nvidia has been charged with any wrongdoing thus far.
A longtime engineer posted to Nvidia's internal suggestion box urging the board to weigh employee sentiment before acting, according to internal correspondence reviewed by Wired .
But the decision rests with Nvidia's board, and it has given no sign of reversing course.
The company is continuing its own investigation into Huang, according to The Information .

13, the board said it was still selecting a search firm for the CEO role and had not formally engaged any potential candidates , after the Financial Times reported that it had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas.
Washington's scrutiny also goes beyond Huang himself: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has questioned whether Nvidia knew who it was selling chips to.
The signers say they haven't been shown evidence that the woman at the center of the controversy was a spy, and argue Huang deserves "due process, not mob justice."
Numbers are moving fast, and this is probably already out of date.
Identities on the site are self-reported, and the list includes entries that appear to be fake or duplicated, including at least one offensive name listed as a current Nvidia employee.
The totals are best read as a rough gauge of support rather than a true headcount.
"Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen," one employee told Wired.

One employee sent a companywide email demanding transparency about Huang's exit, writing: "I stand by Jensen." About two dozen employees posted support on LinkedIn, and Moneywise couldn't find any employee posts backing his departure.
Sam Altman came back within five days, so there's still time to see how this unfolds.
The clock is ticking until Nvidia's Tuesday earnings call.
President Donald Trump called Huang on Tuesday urging him to fight for his job , The New York Times reported.

Elon Musk wants Jensen Huang back in charge of Nvidia [NASDAQ: NVDA] — and he's putting his name on it. "A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I'm signing it too," the Tesla and SpaceX CEO [NASDAQ: TSLA] posted on X on Nov. 13. He isn't alone. As of 10:30 a.m. ET on Nov. 14, an online letter called Stand with Jensen listed more than 100,000 names — including more than 5,000 people who say they currently work at Nvidia. Huang co-founded the chipmaker in 1993 and led it for 33 years, building it into one of the world's most valuable companies. Nvidia announced Nov. 12 that he had resigned as president, CEO and board member , effective immediately. The board accepted his resignation Nov. 11, according to a regulatory filing . CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO , and director Harvey Jones became the board's first-ever chair. His exit came after reports that he'd had extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspect was recruited by China's top spy agency. Huang has admitted to an affair . Neither he nor Nvidia has been charged with any wrongdoing thus far. Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 5 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change The Stand with Jensen letter asks the board to "bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA's best interests." Beyond reinstatement, the letter asks the board to disclose the scope, independence and timeline of its investigation, give Huang a chance to respond before any final decision, and publicly explain the evidence behind his removal. The signers say they haven't been shown evidence that the woman at the center of the controversy was a spy, and argue Huang deserves "due process, not mob justice." The site says it isn't affiliated with Nvidia or Huang. Signers identify themselves, and organizers say they may hold new signatures for review before counting them. At this point, the site's live tracker broke the names down like this: Numbers are moving fast, and this is probably already out of date. For context, Nvidia had about 42,000 employees at the end of its last fiscal year in January, according to its annual report , so the self-identified current staff would represent roughly 12% of the company. Musk is listed at the top as a shareholder, alongside Replit CEO Amjad Masad; Gavin Baker, managing partner of Atreides Management; Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney; and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. Cohere's Aidan Gomez and Serve Robotics CEO Ali Kashani are listed as partners. Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke replied "You have my sword" to Musk's petition post, though Moneywise didn't find his name on the list. Identities on the site are self-reported, and the list includes entries that appear to be fake or duplicated, including at least one offensive name listed as a current Nvidia employee. There's even an unverifiable entry for actress Sydney Sweeney listed as a shareholder. The totals are best read as a rough gauge of support rather than a true headcount. The pushback started inside the company. A longtime engineer posted to Nvidia's internal suggestion box urging the board to weigh employee sentiment before acting, according to internal correspondence reviewed by Wired . The post has drawn more than 1,600 comments, several asking the board to find a way to bring Huang back. One employee sent a companywide email demanding transparency about Huang's exit, writing: "I stand by Jensen." About two dozen employees posted support on LinkedIn, and Moneywise couldn't find any employee posts backing his departure. "Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen," one employee told Wired. In an informal poll, we asked Moneywise followers whether Nvidia should bring Jensen back. Of 164 votes, 82% said "most definitely." Just 6% said "absolutely not," while 12% picked "he's poaching them all," a nod to the idea that Nvidia employees would follow Huang wherever he goes next. The post follows days of public support from Musk. On the night of Nov. 11, before Huang resigned, Musk replied "That would be an honor" to a ZeroHedge post urging him to hire Huang. The next day, he answered "True words" to AngelList co-founder Naval Ravikant, who wrote that "one does not just simply replace the founder," pointing to Steve Jobs and Travis Kalanick. When Ravikant followed up by calling Huang "the Steve Jobs of Nvidia" and "irreplaceable," Musk replied "True." He also replied "Always" to a post praising him for being a true friend to Huang. The two go back years. In May, Musk replied "True" to a repost of photos of the pair taken a decade apart, captioned "The most important thing in life is having true friends." Musk also has a business stake in the outcome. His rocket and AI company, SpaceX [NASDAQ: SPCX], has committed to building its AI data centers exclusively with Nvidia chips, and Nvidia owns a stake in SpaceX worth billions . The petition site also lists him as an Nvidia shareholder. Since resigning, Huang has kept a low profile. Photos published by the Daily Mail show friends and family gathering at what the outlet described as his $38 million Pacific Heights mansion in San Francisco in the hours after he stepped down, as food deliveries, including bags of fried chicken, arrived at the door. Washington isn't done with him. Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Huang agreed to come in . Three House committee chairs then asked him to sit for a closed-door, transcribed interview on Dec. 1, giving him until 8 p.m. ET on Nov. 13 to confirm or face a subpoena. It wasn't immediately clear whether Huang had confirmed in writing by the deadline. Senate Banking Committee chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., has separately asked Huang to testify on Dec. 3. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whom Scott also called to testify, has agreed to appear . The petition's backers argue the board moved before the facts were in, and the central question is still open. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Nov. 12 there had been "no conclusions reached by the Department of Justice, or by me" about whether Alice Huang was a spy, according to Reuters . Beijing has denied that she is one, and President Donald Trump has said it isn't yet clear either way. What is on the record is narrower. Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said Nov. 12 that she has been barred from re-entering the country since February amid an investigation into possible offenses tied to Megaspeed, though it said that investigation did not concern espionage. There's recent precedent. In November 2023, OpenAI's board fired CEO Sam Altman, then reached a deal to bring him back about five days later after hundreds of employees threatened to quit. Even the White House has weighed in on both sides. President Donald Trump called Huang on Tuesday urging him to fight for his job , The New York Times reported. After Huang resigned, Trump posted on Truth Social that there was "only one man to take his place": Apple chairman Tim Cook. But the decision rests with Nvidia's board, and it has given no sign of reversing course. The company is continuing its own investigation into Huang, according to The Information . On Nov. 13, the board said it was still selecting a search firm for the CEO role and had not formally engaged any potential candidates , after the Financial Times reported that it had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas. Washington's scrutiny also goes beyond Huang himself: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has questioned whether Nvidia knew who it was selling chips to. Sam Altman came back within five days, so there's still time to see how this unfolds. The clock is ticking until Nvidia's Tuesday earnings call. Elon Musk wants Jensen Huang back in charge of Nvidia [NASDAQ: NVDA] — and he's putting his name on it.
"A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I'm signing it too," the Tesla and SpaceX CEO [NASDAQ: TSLA] posted on X on Nov. 13.
He isn't alone. As of 10:30 a.m. ET on Nov. 14, an online letter called Stand with Jensen listed more than 100,000 names — including more than 5,000 people who say they currently work at Nvidia.

Huang co-founded the chipmaker in 1993 and led it for 33 years, building it into one of the world's most valuable companies. Nvidia announced Nov. 12 that he had resigned as president, CEO and board member , effective immediately. The board accepted his resignation Nov. 11, according to a regulatory filing . CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO , and director Harvey Jones became the board's first-ever chair.

His exit came after reports that he'd had extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspect was recruited by China's top spy agency. Huang has admitted to an affair . Neither he nor Nvidia has been charged with any wrongdoing thus far.

The Stand with Jensen letter asks the board to "bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA's best interests."

Beyond reinstatement, the letter asks the board to disclose the scope, independence and timeline of its investigation, give Huang a chance to respond before any final decision, and publicly explain the evidence behind his removal. The signers say they haven't been shown evidence that the woman at the center of the controversy was a spy, and argue Huang deserves "due process, not mob justice."
The site says it isn't affiliated with Nvidia or Huang. Signers identify themselves, and organizers say they may hold new signatures for review before counting them.
At this point, the site's live tracker broke the names down like this:

Numbers are moving fast, and this is probably already out of date. For context, Nvidia had about 42,000 employees at the end of its last fiscal year in January, according to its annual report , so the self-identified current staff would represent roughly 12% of the company.

Musk is listed at the top as a shareholder, alongside Replit CEO Amjad Masad; Gavin Baker, managing partner of Atreides Management; Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney; and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. Cohere's Aidan Gomez and Serve Robotics CEO Ali Kashani are listed as partners. Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke replied "You have my sword" to Musk's petition post, though Moneywise didn't find his name on the list.

Identities on the site are self-reported, and the list includes entries that appear to be fake or duplicated, including at least one offensive name listed as a current Nvidia employee. There's even an unverifiable entry for actress Sydney Sweeney listed as a shareholder. The totals are best read as a rough gauge of support rather than a true headcount.

The pushback started inside the company. A longtime engineer posted to Nvidia's internal suggestion box urging the board to weigh employee sentiment before acting, according to internal correspondence reviewed by Wired . The post has drawn more than 1,600 comments, several asking the board to find a way to bring Huang back.

One employee sent a companywide email demanding transparency about Huang's exit, writing: "I stand by Jensen." About two dozen employees posted support on LinkedIn, and Moneywise couldn't find any employee posts backing his departure.
"Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen," one employee told Wired.

In an informal poll, we asked Moneywise followers whether Nvidia should bring Jensen back. Of 164 votes, 82% said "most definitely." Just 6% said "absolutely not," while 12% picked "he's poaching them all," a nod to the idea that Nvidia employees would follow Huang wherever he goes next.

The post follows days of public support from Musk. On the night of Nov. 11, before Huang resigned, Musk replied "That would be an honor" to a ZeroHedge post urging him to hire Huang. The next day, he answered "True words" to AngelList co-founder Naval Ravikant, who wrote that "one does not just simply replace the founder," pointing to Steve Jobs and Travis Kalanick.
When Ravikant followed up by calling Huang "the Steve Jobs of Nvidia" and "irreplaceable," Musk replied "True." He also replied "Always" to a post praising him for being a true friend to Huang.
The two go back years. In May, Musk replied "True" to a repost of photos of the pair taken a decade apart, captioned "The most important thing in life is having true friends."

Musk also has a business stake in the outcome. His rocket and AI company, SpaceX [NASDAQ: SPCX], has committed to building its AI data centers exclusively with Nvidia chips, and Nvidia owns a stake in SpaceX worth billions . The petition site also lists him as an Nvidia shareholder.

Since resigning, Huang has kept a low profile. Photos published by the Daily Mail show friends and family gathering at what the outlet described as his $38 million Pacific Heights mansion in San Francisco in the hours after he stepped down, as food deliveries, including bags of fried chicken, arrived at the door.

Washington isn't done with him. Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Huang agreed to come in . Three House committee chairs then asked him to sit for a closed-door, transcribed interview on Dec. 1, giving him until 8 p.m. ET on Nov. 13 to confirm or face a subpoena. It wasn't immediately clear whether Huang had confirmed in writing by the deadline.
Senate Banking Committee chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., has separately asked Huang to testify on Dec. 3. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whom Scott also called to testify, has agreed to appear .

The petition's backers argue the board moved before the facts were in, and the central question is still open. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Nov. 12 there had been "no conclusions reached by the Department of Justice, or by me" about whether Alice Huang was a spy, according to Reuters . Beijing has denied that she is one, and President Donald Trump has said it isn't yet clear either way.

What is on the record is narrower. Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said Nov. 12 that she has been barred from re-entering the country since February amid an investigation into possible offenses tied to Megaspeed, though it said that investigation did not concern espionage.
There's recent precedent. In November 2023, OpenAI's board fired CEO Sam Altman, then reached a deal to bring him back about five days later after hundreds of employees threatened to quit.

Even the White House has weighed in on both sides. President Donald Trump called Huang on Tuesday urging him to fight for his job , The New York Times reported. After Huang resigned, Trump posted on Truth Social that there was "only one man to take his place": Apple chairman Tim Cook.

But the decision rests with Nvidia's board, and it has given no sign of reversing course. The company is continuing its own investigation into Huang, according to The Information . On Nov. 13, the board said it was still selecting a search firm for the CEO role and had not formally engaged any potential candidates , after the Financial Times reported that it had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas. Washington's scrutiny also goes beyond Huang himself: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has questioned whether Nvidia knew who it was selling chips to.
Sam Altman came back within five days, so there's still time to see how this unfolds. The clock is ticking until Nvidia's Tuesday earnings call.

Elon Musk wants Jensen Huang back in charge of Nvidia [NASDAQ: NVDA] — and he's putting his name on it. "A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I'm signing it too," the Tesla and SpaceX CEO [NASDAQ: TSLA] posted on X on Nov. 13. He isn't alone. As of 10:30 a.m. ET on Nov. 14, an online letter called Stand with Jensen listed more than 100,000 names — including more than 5,000 people who say they currently work at Nvidia. Huang co-founded the chipmaker in 1993 and led it for 33 years, building it into one of the world's most valuable companies. Nvidia announced Nov. 12 that he had resigned as president, CEO and board member , effective immediately. The board accepted his resignation Nov. 11, according to a regulatory filing . CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO , and director Harvey Jones became the board's first-ever chair. His exit came after reports that he'd had extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspect was recruited by China's top spy agency. Huang has admitted to an affair . Neither he nor Nvidia has been charged with any wrongdoing thus far. Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 5 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change The Stand with Jensen letter asks the board to "bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA's best interests." Beyond reinstatement, the letter asks the board to disclose the scope, independence and timeline of its investigation, give Huang a chance to respond before any final decision, and publicly explain the evidence behind his removal. The signers say they haven't been shown evidence that the woman at the center of the controversy was a spy, and argue Huang deserves "due process, not mob justice." The site says it isn't affiliated with Nvidia or Huang. Signers identify themselves, and organizers say they may hold new signatures for review before counting them. At this point, the site's live tracker broke the names down like this: Numbers are moving fast, and this is probably already out of date. For context, Nvidia had about 42,000 employees at the end of its last fiscal year in January, according to its annual report , so the self-identified current staff would represent roughly 12% of the company. Musk is listed at the top as a shareholder, alongside Replit CEO Amjad Masad; Gavin Baker, managing partner of Atreides Management; Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney; and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. Cohere's Aidan Gomez and Serve Robotics CEO Ali Kashani are listed as partners. Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke replied "You have my sword" to Musk's petition post, though Moneywise didn't find his name on the list. Identities on the site are self-reported, and the list includes entries that appear to be fake or duplicated, including at least one offensive name listed as a current Nvidia employee. There's even an unverifiable entry for actress Sydney Sweeney listed as a shareholder. The totals are best read as a rough gauge of support rather than a true headcount. The pushback started inside the company. A longtime engineer posted to Nvidia's internal suggestion box urging the board to weigh employee sentiment before acting, according to internal correspondence reviewed by Wired . The post has drawn more than 1,600 comments, several asking the board to find a way to bring Huang back. One employee sent a companywide email demanding transparency about Huang's exit, writing: "I stand by Jensen." About two dozen employees posted support on LinkedIn, and Moneywise couldn't find any employee posts backing his departure. "Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen," one employee told Wired. In an informal poll, we asked Moneywise followers whether Nvidia should bring Jensen back. Of 164 votes, 82% said "most definitely." Just 6% said "absolutely not," while 12% picked "he's poaching them all," a nod to the idea that Nvidia employees would follow Huang wherever he goes next. The post follows days of public support from Musk. On the night of Nov. 11, before Huang resigned, Musk replied "That would be an honor" to a ZeroHedge post urging him to hire Huang. The next day, he answered "True words" to AngelList co-founder Naval Ravikant, who wrote that "one does not just simply replace the founder," pointing to Steve Jobs and Travis Kalanick. When Ravikant followed up by calling Huang "the Steve Jobs of Nvidia" and "irreplaceable," Musk replied "True." He also replied "Always" to a post praising him for being a true friend to Huang. The two go back years. In May, Musk replied "True" to a repost of photos of the pair taken a decade apart, captioned "The most important thing in life is having true friends." Musk also has a business stake in the outcome. His rocket and AI company, SpaceX [NASDAQ: SPCX], has committed to building its AI data centers exclusively with Nvidia chips, and Nvidia owns a stake in SpaceX worth billions . The petition site also lists him as an Nvidia shareholder. Since resigning, Huang has kept a low profile. Photos published by the Daily Mail show friends and family gathering at what the outlet described as his $38 million Pacific Heights mansion in San Francisco in the hours after he stepped down, as food deliveries, including bags of fried chicken, arrived at the door. Washington isn't done with him. Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Huang agreed to come in . Three House committee chairs then asked him to sit for a closed-door, transcribed interview on Dec. 1, giving him until 8 p.m. ET on Nov. 13 to confirm or face a subpoena. It wasn't immediately clear whether Huang had confirmed in writing by the deadline. Senate Banking Committee chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., has separately asked Huang to testify on Dec. 3. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whom Scott also called to testify, has agreed to appear . The petition's backers argue the board moved before the facts were in, and the central question is still open. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Nov. 12 there had been "no conclusions reached by the Department of Justice, or by me" about whether Alice Huang was a spy, according to Reuters . Beijing has denied that she is one, and President Donald Trump has said it isn't yet clear either way. What is on the record is narrower. Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said Nov. 12 that she has been barred from re-entering the country since February amid an investigation into possible offenses tied to Megaspeed, though it said that investigation did not concern espionage. There's recent precedent. In November 2023, OpenAI's board fired CEO Sam Altman, then reached a deal to bring him back about five days later after hundreds of employees threatened to quit. Even the White House has weighed in on both sides. President Donald Trump called Huang on Tuesday urging him to fight for his job , The New York Times reported. After Huang resigned, Trump posted on Truth Social that there was "only one man to take his place": Apple chairman Tim Cook. But the decision rests with Nvidia's board, and it has given no sign of reversing course. The company is continuing its own investigation into Huang, according to The Information . On Nov. 13, the board said it was still selecting a search firm for the CEO role and had not formally engaged any potential candidates , after the Financial Times reported that it had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas. Washington's scrutiny also goes beyond Huang himself: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has questioned whether Nvidia knew who it was selling chips to. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang. “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another. One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.” The employee couldn’t be reached for comment, while the engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment. Nvidia and its new board chair, investor Harvey Jones, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, following reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report. (This employee has not commented on the matter.) Since then, Reuters reported on an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn’t commented about these reports since his Sunday email. Are you a current or former Nvidia employee who wants to talk about what’s happening? Nvidia’s board is largely made up of early Nvidia investors and Huang’s longtime confidants. It named Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO and appointed former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones as chair of the board. The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips. It’s been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang’s resignation left many employees stunned. In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation. One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn’t authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang’s reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. “Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” the employee tells WIRED. extraction.body: Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Replit CEO Amjad Masad are among the signers of an online petition asking Nvidia 's board to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive while an independent investigation runs, TechCrunch reported on Saturday, Nov. 14 [1] . Musk said on X on Friday that he had signed the petition, CNBC reported [3] . The "Stand with Jensen" open letter at standwithjensen.com showed 126,753 signatures at 8:49 p.m. ET on Saturday, according to the site's own counter, up from 118,895 at 5:48 p.m. ET and about 97,000 that morning reported by Business Insider [2] [4] . Of those, 6,410 signers described themselves as current Nvidia employees, by the site's tally [2] . The Information reported on Saturday night that thousands of people identifying as Nvidia staff had signed [10] . The site says affiliations are self-reported and not verified, and MLQ.ai has not verified the count or who signed [2] . The letter says its signers are "concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process" and asks the board to "bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts," to ensure a fair investigation and to give the public more information, TechCrunch reported [1] . In a section it labels "Campaign position (not independently verified here)," the site says: "We have not been shown evidence substantiating the espionage allegation" and "Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice" [2] . By the site's tally at 8:49 p.m. ET, signers included 6,410 people describing themselves as current Nvidia employees, 1,208 former employees, 69,172 shareholders and 49,963 other supporters [2] . The site calls itself "an independent, volunteer campaign" not affiliated with or endorsed by Nvidia or Huang, says "affiliations are self-reported and not verified," and says only approved signatures are counted [2] . It does not name its organizers. Its public signer list includes entries for Musk, Masad, Sweeney and Y Combinator's Garry Tan, each listed as a shareholder, and for Atreides Management's Gavin Baker, who co-wrote a separate Nov. 13 letter with Altimeter's Brad Gerstner asking the board to keep "the potential return of Jensen Huang" among its options ( our report ) [2] [3] . Musk also said on X on Saturday that without Huang some "critical deals will be lost," CNBC reported [3] . Nvidia's board accepted Huang's resignation as CEO and director on Nov. 11 and named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO; the company's 8-K gives no reason and describes no disagreement with the board [5] . CNBC, citing a person familiar with the matter, reported that the board had decided to oust him [7] . Reuters reported that pressure mounted after reports of his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive of Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom US authorities have investigated on suspicion of spying for China; Beijing denies she is a spy, and she has not been charged [7] [8] . Huang acknowledged in a Nov. 8 message to staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife, and he has denied compromising national security or Nvidia secrets, CNBC reported [7] . Reuters also reported on Nov. 13 that Huang misled Nvidia's general counsel about the relationship; Nvidia and a Huang representative declined to comment ( our report ) [8] . Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Nov. 12 that the Justice Department had reached "no conclusions" about who Alice Huang "is or is not" ( our report ) [9] . The board has not responded publicly to the petition or the investor letter [6] . The independent directors' investigation, run by Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz and former acting US Attorney Joon H. Kim, is continuing, with no published timeline [6] . Neither Huang nor Nvidia has commented on the petition [1] . MLQ.ai's explainer on what a return would require sets out the board's powers, and the Nvidia scandal story page has the full timeline [6] . Nvidia reports fiscal third-quarter results on Tuesday, Nov. 17, its first under Kress, and holds a company meeting for staff on Nov. 18 [5] [7] . extraction.body: If I'd told you this time last week that Jensen Huang was about to leave Nvidia, you would not have believed me. The man who co-founded this enormously successful AI chip company, working tirelessly to build it from the ground up and steering it through some disastrous times with endless energy and ruthless determination, has ultimately been undone by his own love life. It's an extraordinary tale and a strangely old fashioned one for a tech firm with its sights set on the future. It spawned a plethora of viral memes, seeing Huang as the man caught by the Coldplay kiss-cam with a married colleague , or singing along to George Michael's classic hit about betrayal, Careless Whisper. Both were ironically AI-generated using the very tech he was helping to build. This week I met two Silicon Valley execs and I asked them how they were processing the news - "in memes", was the response. But they didn't seem to think Huang would be forced out by his alleged adultery. The stakes were too high, they said, the entire AI industry relies too heavily on Nvidia chips to break a winning formula. In as many words, "the Valley" was on his side. But that was before rumours of a second affair surfaced, this time with a colleague, and the board decided he had gone too far. His behaviour suddenly cast him in a different light: a man who could make bad decisions and cover them up. Huang always made a point of standing out from the crowd. During the coronavirus lockdowns, he streamed keynote speeches from his kitchen (which gained internet fame in its own right, but were later revealed to have been AI-generated). He is rarely seen without a leather jacket – he has joked that he only owns one suit, and he borrows his daughter's partner's tie. Huang rubbed shoulders with the elite, with a network including Donald Trump, Elon Musk and King Charles. The last time I saw him was at St James' Palace last year, where he was receiving the prestigious Queen's Prize for Engineering. I was told he would not talk to the press - but he wandered over by himself and we spent about 10 minutes having a chat while press officers hovered nervously in the background. He was articulate and optimistic about the progress of AI and the UK's role in it. For many people, Huang was Nvidia. He had as many as 200 people directly reporting to him. He expected high standards – in his book about its inner workings, the Nvidia Way, author Tae Kim wrote the office hours were long. Huang's feedback could be both brutal and public, and he thought nothing of pointing out individuals' mistakes in all-staff meetings. Now it is his own shortcomings which are on very public display, and he has been forced into a brutal ending of his own career. Colette Kress, who takes over for now, will be a familiar face internally and that must feel reassuring to some at Nvidia. She's worked at the company for 13 years and for those who follow its considerable finances, she is often present on earnings calls. She is a billionaire in her own right and a high-flying tech executive. But she's not an engineer and Nvidia's products are highly technical. She will have to convince investors that it is business as usual for Nvidia, that the innovation for which it is renowned can continue at its existing pace, and that the top talent won't leave with Huang. A wobbly Nvidia would be bad news for the entire AI industry because its ever-advancing chips drive the most powerful AI models, and it's also regarded as something of a central bank, loaning money to other firms. As for Huang himself, we assume for now that the investigation into his relationship with the woman accused of being a Chinese spy will continue, and the results of that may well determine what he does next. He probably won't be short of offers despite his conduct – and I expect Nvidia's rivals can't believe their luck that their formidable rival has taken himself out of the game. Elon Musk has already said it would be "an honour" to work with him at SpaceX. It's important though to remember that even if Huang turns out not to have betrayed his company or his country, he still betrayed his wife of 41 years, Lori Huang. And for her, it's not a story of tech, temptation and trillion-dollar-valuations. The scandal has cast a spotlight on Singapore's success as a chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade. Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs. BBC's Asma Khalid explains how the Nvidia affair could threaten US national security and risk sensitive US technology getting into China. Within days, Huang's status as a seemingly untouchable figure leading the global tech race has crumbled. It's an extraordinary tale and a strangely old fashioned one for a tech firm with its sights set on the future.

It spawned a plethora of viral memes, seeing Huang as the man caught by the Coldplay kiss-cam with a married colleague , or singing along to George Michael's classic hit about betrayal, Careless Whisper.
Both were ironically AI-generated using the very tech he was helping to build.
This week I met two Silicon Valley execs and I asked them how they were processing the news - "in memes", was the response.
But they didn't seem to think Huang would be forced out by his alleged adultery.
The stakes were too high, they said, the entire AI industry relies too heavily on Nvidia chips to break a winning formula.
In as many words, "the Valley" was on his side.
But that was before rumours of a second affair surfaced, this time with a colleague, and the board decided he had gone too far.
His behaviour suddenly cast him in a different light: a man who could make bad decisions and cover them up.
Huang always made a point of standing out from the crowd.
During the coronavirus lockdowns, he streamed keynote speeches from his kitchen (which gained internet fame in its own right, but were later revealed to have been AI-generated).
He is rarely seen without a leather jacket – he has joked that he only owns one suit, and he borrows his daughter's partner's tie.
Huang rubbed shoulders with the elite, with a network including Donald Trump, Elon Musk and King Charles.
The last time I saw him was at St James' Palace last year, where he was receiving the prestigious Queen's Prize for Engineering.

I was told he would not talk to the press - but he wandered over by himself and we spent about 10 minutes having a chat while press officers hovered nervously in the background. He was articulate and optimistic about the progress of AI and the UK's role in it.
For many people, Huang was Nvidia. He had as many as 200 people directly reporting to him.
He expected high standards – in his book about its inner workings, the Nvidia Way, author Tae Kim wrote the office hours were long.
Huang's feedback could be both brutal and public, and he thought nothing of pointing out individuals' mistakes in all-staff meetings.
Now it is his own shortcomings which are on very public display, and he has been forced into a brutal ending of his own career.
Colette Kress, who takes over for now, will be a familiar face internally and that must feel reassuring to some at Nvidia.

She's worked at the company for 13 years and for those who follow its considerable finances, she is often present on earnings calls. She is a billionaire in her own right and a high-flying tech executive.
But she's not an engineer and Nvidia's products are highly technical.

She will have to convince investors that it is business as usual for Nvidia, that the innovation for which it is renowned can continue at its existing pace, and that the top talent won't leave with Huang.

A wobbly Nvidia would be bad news for the entire AI industry because its ever-advancing chips drive the most powerful AI models, and it's also regarded as something of a central bank, loaning money to other firms.

As for Huang himself, we assume for now that the investigation into his relationship with the woman accused of being a Chinese spy will continue, and the results of that may well determine what he does next.

He probably won't be short of offers despite his conduct – and I expect Nvidia's rivals can't believe their luck that their formidable rival has taken himself out of the game. Elon Musk has already said it would be "an honour" to work with him at SpaceX.
It's important though to remember that even if Huang turns out not to have betrayed his company or his country, he still betrayed his wife of 41 years, Lori Huang.
And for her, it's not a story of tech, temptation and trillion-dollar-valuations.
The scandal has cast a spotlight on Singapore's success as a chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.
Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs.
BBC's Asma Khalid explains how the Nvidia affair could threaten US national security and risk sensitive US technology getting into China.
Within days, Huang's status as a seemingly untouchable figure leading the global tech race has crumbled.
