extraction.body: I had agreed to travel to Denver, Colorado, to interview the Nvidia CEO at SIGGRAPH, the annual confab of computer graphics PhDs and practitioners. Early that year I’d conducted a lengthy sit-down interview with Huang for a WIRED magazine feature, which apparently went well enough—both for WIRED and for Nvidia’s executive communications team—that I had been asked to interview Huang again at this conference. Another opportunity to grill the CEO of the modern world’s most consequential company? She told me about the slides Jensen would be presenting on stage at SIGGRAPH and offered suggestions for key moments when I might tee him up to talk about the slides. I raised my concerns with both my editors and Nvidia. We agreed that I would ask the questions I intended to ask him, which included questions about the environmental impact of data centers, and that Huang would also be referring to slides. Let’s just say the interview didn’t go smoothly. (It’s on YouTube.) To this day, former and current Nvidia workers sometimes tell me that I “handled” the whole thing well. Huang was domineering, evaded some of my questions, and, immediately after our session concluded, did an impromptu Q&A session with a much more adoring crowd than me. Then I was guided offstage, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg hopped on, where he and Huang had a lovey-dovey fireside chat. Huang later agreed to meet with me again, in December 2024. But that interview in Denver had underscored for me how much Jensen Huang wanted to control the narrative. Narrative has always been a critical part of Huang’s success. He was not just your average electrical engineering nerd who toiled away on something that would eventually find a product-market fit. By Huang’s own telling, he was an immigrant founder, an underdog, a wife guy who chased (and eventually married) his college sweetheart, a scrappy startup guy who dined at Denny’s in the early days. A visionary who worked Sundays and who didn’t sleep well because he always heard the hoof steps of competitors. A man who loved Nvidia so much he tattooed an abstract version of the company logo on his arm. Huang built the highest-valued publicly traded company in history. Back in January 2024, when I sat down with him for our first-ever in-person meeting, Huang right off the bat talked about the importance of storytelling. Here’s an excerpt: Jensen Huang: Somebody who I really admire, as a leader and a person, is Shantanu Narayen, the CEO of Adobe. He said he always wanted to be a journalist because he loved telling stories. WIRED: It seems like an important part of building a business, being able to tell its story effectively. You’ve said many times you didn’t sell the idea of Nvidia based on a pitch deck. Of course, even then, Huang was caught up in the crosshairs of the US–China AI war and at the mercy of regulators, as I wrote at the time. After Donald Trump’s reelection that year, Huang once again deployed his storytelling skills and lobbied the Trump administration to loosen export controls, so he could sell some of his company’s chips to China. Another crucial part of the Huang lore is that he ran a “flat” organization, with a few dozen top executives reporting to him. (This is sometimes reported as being “60” people; insiders have told me at times it’s closer to 35.) Huang once said the structure allowed Nvidia “to adapt a lot more quickly, which we need because our technology is moving so quickly.” Huang was also known to be controlling of all aspects of the business—participating in every significant meeting, seemingly aware of every moving part, and staying in the loop on sourcing, supply chains, and the company’s allocation of chips. This is where Huang’s cult of leadership, and his Nvidia storytelling, may have come to a stupidly disappointing final chapter. As one former employee put it, Huang can’t simultaneously have had knowledge of every element of Nvidia’s business and then potentially feign ignorance about where the chips may have fallen, both figuratively and literally. His apparent lapses in judgment have now led him to resign from the very company he coaxed into existence and have shattered the mythos of its ever-prescient founder. It’s certainly not the narrative ending Huang would have chosen, were he still in control.

extraction.body: On January 6th, 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got his rockstar moment at last. He has left Nvidia after seemingly enabling two chip smuggling scandals and allegedly having three extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy at the same time he was mingling with President Donald Trump. That’s because Huang wasn’t merely running the first $5 trillion company, he was the visionary leader in control of the must-have GPUs powering the worldwide AI boom, part of a company that represents around 6 percent of the S&P 500 stock market index all by itself. The 63-year-old once said he preferred to die on the job; he once suggested he’d work until he was 90 or 100, then carry on leading the company as a robot. It’s not easy to replace Huang, partly because he had no deputies. Around 60 employees reported directly to the CEO. “He built the company around himself, and everything that happened there flowed through him,” says IDC analyst and former computing journalist Tom Mainelli. “Jensen is Nvidia, and Nvidia is Jensen,” Jon Peddie, a computer industry analyst who’s been tracking Nvidia since its inception, tells me. He has left the company he cofounded 33 years ago. It’s the end of an era, and not just for Nvidia — because Jensen Huang was Big Tech’s last true example of a visionary showman founder CEO. “He was both the visionary and the tactical leader, the closest thing tech has had to Steve Jobs,” Moor Insights & Strategy chief analyst Pat Moorhead tells me. Elon Musk didn’t exactly found Tesla and has quite the track record of broken promises, and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg has proven to be neither visionary nor showman so far. Google’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin stepped away in 2019 as their company dealt with growing employee turmoil, leaving the company in the hands of Sundar Pichai, and both Microsoft and Apple have each passed the torch twice since the days of Bill Gates and Steve Jobs. Some say Apple’s Steve Jobs broke the CEO mold, but he created a mold of his own. Huang was one of countless tech leaders who followed his example by introducing their products in keynote speeches, adopting a single recognizable piece of clothing like Jobs’ trademark black turtleneck, and even occasionally teasing “one more thing” for the surprise at the end of their presentations. I thought Huang might be a Jobs wannabe, too, the first time I saw that he’d adopted a black jacket as his uniform. (It was not always a leather jacket; an earlier version was a Nvidia-branded softshell.) Huang later insisted on wearing a jacket even when the temperature was hot — more than once, I saw him sweat profusely rather than take it off. Unlike Jobs, he also held quite a few keynotes when he didn’t have much news to share; he liked to repeat the company’s previous accomplishments as if they were brand-new. But even if Huang didn’t have the same gravitas as Jobs, he did have exciting tech up his sleeves and loved to demo it onstage. He took Nvidia to fame and fortune through a series of tremendous bets. In 1996, three years after he cofounded the company at a Denny’s diner, Nvidia nearly went out of business while working on a failed graphics chip for the Sega Dreamcast game console. But even though he didn’t deliver that chip, Huang personally convinced Sega to invest $5 million afterward, The Wall Street Journal reported in 2024. He then turned around and bet the company again on the Riva 128 PC graphics accelerator, an effort so ambitious he had to lay off over half of Nvidia’s roughly 100 staffers, skip the prototyping stage, and rush it straight to production, and he still only had one month of payroll left by the time it shipped, The New Yorker wrote in 2023. Thankfully, it was a success, selling a million units in just four months and paving the way for both the GeForce GPU and a long-term relationship with chip fabricator TSMC. Roughly eight years later, Huang decided it wasn’t enough to be the leader in PC gaming graphics alone. He bet the company’s entire gross profit, he told podcaster Lex Fridman, on shipping a new feature inside those graphics cards that no one had asked for: CUDA. It was the ability to use a GPU for other kinds of computing tasks beyond graphics, and Huang said it increased the cost of every GeForce graphics card by 50 percent. “Jensen had the vision for what it could be and the courage to pursue it in spite of the opinions of others.” “NVIDIA was effectively investing in a computing platform that extended far beyond graphics, with no guarantee of a near-term return,” says HotTech analyst Dave Altavilla. “Huang saw that a GPU was really a parallel computer that happened to render graphics. CUDA turned that insight into a platform, and it’s why NVIDIA was ready when AI arrived,” Mainelli tells me. When the Great Recession hit in 2007–2009, and Nvidia laptop graphics chips also started failing due to design defects, the company lost 80 percent of its market value. But Huang believed in CUDA enough to invest even more. “He literally handed out high-end NVIDIA GPUs to researchers at industry conferences, while the company seeded universities like Stanford with hardware to encourage development on its platform,” says Altavilla. And by 2012, Nvidia’s potential for AI had started to emerge. That’s when University of Toronto researchers used Nvidia GPUs to train a prize-winning image-recognition neural network called AlexNet, which is widely credited for sparking the AI revolution. Not all of Huang’s visions panned out the way he publicly expected. That AlexNet demo directly led to Huang’s bets on chips for self-driving cars, he said, but he didn’t exactly predict AI — CUDA was instead thought of as better and more affordable supercomputing for researchers and scientists.

sources.title: The Swift Downfall of Jensen Huang and What’s Next for Nvidia - New York Magazine
passages: Less than two weeks ago, billionaire Jensen Huang was a gainfully employed CEO whose personal life the general public knew very little about; today, he’s out at Nvidia, the multitrillion-dollar company he co-founded in 1993, following revelations that he had an affair with (1) a woman accused of being a Chinese spy and (2) an Nvidia subordinate.

The stunning downfall will undoubtedly have reverberations far beyond Nvidia’s Silicon Valley campus, given Huang’s position as one of the most powerful, if not the most powerful, figures in the AI industry and his close proximity to Donald Trump.
On Wall Street, the company’s stock was down 11 percent on the news of his departure, which translates to a loss of roughly $1 trillion just this month.

In Washington, the New York Times notes that few tech executives “have had as much sway as Huang over Trump’s approach to A.I. and China.” He reportedly “persuaded the president to roll back a ban on chip sales to China and Nvidia has donated at least $20 million to a fund for Trump’s White House ballroom project.”

On Wednesday Nvidia’s board met for hours to decide Huang’s fate, and, despite the CEO reportedly “fighting hard to hang onto his role with the company he founded,” Huang resigned Thursday morning and chief financial officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO.

Incredibly, Nvidia had no successor in place prior to the scandal that took down its leader because Huang didn’t believe in succession planning ; he was also apparently a micromanager with 60 direct reports and said last year that he reads thousands of employee emails a day.

Around 60 employees reported directly to the CEO.

extraction.body: If I'd told you this time last week that Jensen Huang was about to leave Nvidia, you would not have believed me. The man who co-founded this enormously successful AI chip company, working tirelessly to build it from the ground up and steering it through some disastrous times with endless energy and ruthless determination, has ultimately been undone by his own love life. It's an extraordinary tale and a strangely old fashioned one for a tech firm with its sights set on the future. It spawned a plethora of viral memes, seeing Huang as the man caught by the Coldplay kiss-cam with a married colleague , or singing along to George Michael's classic hit about betrayal, Careless Whisper. Both were ironically AI-generated using the very tech he was helping to build. This week I met two Silicon Valley execs and I asked them how they were processing the news - "in memes", was the response. But they didn't seem to think Huang would be forced out by his alleged adultery. The stakes were too high, they said, the entire AI industry relies too heavily on Nvidia chips to break a winning formula. In as many words, "the Valley" was on his side. But that was before rumours of a second affair surfaced, this time with a colleague, and the board decided he had gone too far. His behaviour suddenly cast him in a different light: a man who could make bad decisions and cover them up. Huang always made a point of standing out from the crowd. During the coronavirus lockdowns, he streamed keynote speeches from his kitchen (which gained internet fame in its own right, but were later revealed to have been AI-generated). He is rarely seen without a leather jacket – he has joked that he only owns one suit, and he borrows his daughter's partner's tie. Huang rubbed shoulders with the elite, with a network including Donald Trump, Elon Musk and King Charles. The last time I saw him was at St James' Palace last year, where he was receiving the prestigious Queen's Prize for Engineering. I was told he would not talk to the press - but he wandered over by himself and we spent about 10 minutes having a chat while press officers hovered nervously in the background. He was articulate and optimistic about the progress of AI and the UK's role in it. For many people, Huang was Nvidia. He had as many as 200 people directly reporting to him. He expected high standards – in his book about its inner workings, the Nvidia Way, author Tae Kim wrote the office hours were long. Huang's feedback could be both brutal and public, and he thought nothing of pointing out individuals' mistakes in all-staff meetings. Now it is his own shortcomings which are on very public display, and he has been forced into a brutal ending of his own career. Colette Kress, who takes over for now, will be a familiar face internally and that must feel reassuring to some at Nvidia. She's worked at the company for 13 years and for those who follow its considerable finances, she is often present on earnings calls. She is a billionaire in her own right and a high-flying tech executive. But she's not an engineer and Nvidia's products are highly technical. She will have to convince investors that it is business as usual for Nvidia, that the innovation for which it is renowned can continue at its existing pace, and that the top talent won't leave with Huang. A wobbly Nvidia would be bad news for the entire AI industry because its ever-advancing chips drive the most powerful AI models, and it's also regarded as something of a central bank, loaning money to other firms. As for Huang himself, we assume for now that the investigation into his relationship with the woman accused of being a Chinese spy will continue, and the results of that may well determine what he does next. He probably won't be short of offers despite his conduct – and I expect Nvidia's rivals can't believe their luck that their formidable rival has taken himself out of the game. Elon Musk has already said it would be "an honour" to work with him at SpaceX. It's important though to remember that even if Huang turns out not to have betrayed his company or his country, he still betrayed his wife of 41 years, Lori Huang. And for her, it's not a story of tech, temptation and trillion-dollar-valuations. The scandal has cast a spotlight on Singapore's success as a chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade. Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs. BBC's Asma Khalid explains how the Nvidia affair could threaten US national security and risk sensitive US technology getting into China. Within days, Huang's status as a seemingly untouchable figure leading the global tech race has crumbled. extraction.body: I had agreed to travel to Denver, Colorado, to interview the Nvidia CEO at SIGGRAPH, the annual confab of computer graphics PhDs and practitioners. Early that year I’d conducted a lengthy sit-down interview with Huang for a WIRED magazine feature, which apparently went well enough—both for WIRED and for Nvidia’s executive communications team—that I had been asked to interview Huang again at this conference. Another opportunity to grill the CEO of the modern world’s most consequential company? She told me about the slides Jensen would be presenting on stage at SIGGRAPH and offered suggestions for key moments when I might tee him up to talk about the slides. I raised my concerns with both my editors and Nvidia. We agreed that I would ask the questions I intended to ask him, which included questions about the environmental impact of data centers, and that Huang would also be referring to slides. Let’s just say the interview didn’t go smoothly. (It’s on YouTube.) To this day, former and current Nvidia workers sometimes tell me that I “handled” the whole thing well. Huang was domineering, evaded some of my questions, and, immediately after our session concluded, did an impromptu Q&A session with a much more adoring crowd than me. Then I was guided offstage, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg hopped on, where he and Huang had a lovey-dovey fireside chat. Huang later agreed to meet with me again, in December 2024. But that interview in Denver had underscored for me how much Jensen Huang wanted to control the narrative. Narrative has always been a critical part of Huang’s success. He was not just your average electrical engineering nerd who toiled away on something that would eventually find a product-market fit. By Huang’s own telling, he was an immigrant founder, an underdog, a wife guy who chased (and eventually married) his college sweetheart, a scrappy startup guy who dined at Denny’s in the early days. A visionary who worked Sundays and who didn’t sleep well because he always heard the hoof steps of competitors. A man who loved Nvidia so much he tattooed an abstract version of the company logo on his arm. Huang built the highest-valued publicly traded company in history. Back in January 2024, when I sat down with him for our first-ever in-person meeting, Huang right off the bat talked about the importance of storytelling. Here’s an excerpt: Jensen Huang: Somebody who I really admire, as a leader and a person, is Shantanu Narayen, the CEO of Adobe. He said he always wanted to be a journalist because he loved telling stories. WIRED: It seems like an important part of building a business, being able to tell its story effectively. You’ve said many times you didn’t sell the idea of Nvidia based on a pitch deck. Of course, even then, Huang was caught up in the crosshairs of the US–China AI war and at the mercy of regulators, as I wrote at the time. After Donald Trump’s reelection that year, Huang once again deployed his storytelling skills and lobbied the Trump administration to loosen export controls, so he could sell some of his company’s chips to China. Another crucial part of the Huang lore is that he ran a “flat” organization, with a few dozen top executives reporting to him. (This is sometimes reported as being “60” people; insiders have told me at times it’s closer to 35.) Huang once said the structure allowed Nvidia “to adapt a lot more quickly, which we need because our technology is moving so quickly.” Huang was also known to be controlling of all aspects of the business—participating in every significant meeting, seemingly aware of every moving part, and staying in the loop on sourcing, supply chains, and the company’s allocation of chips. This is where Huang’s cult of leadership, and his Nvidia storytelling, may have come to a stupidly disappointing final chapter. As one former employee put it, Huang can’t simultaneously have had knowledge of every element of Nvidia’s business and then potentially feign ignorance about where the chips may have fallen, both figuratively and literally. His apparent lapses in judgment have now led him to resign from the very company he coaxed into existence and have shattered the mythos of its ever-prescient founder. It’s certainly not the narrative ending Huang would have chosen, were he still in control.

extraction.body: On January 6th, 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got his rockstar moment at last. He has left Nvidia after seemingly enabling two chip smuggling scandals and allegedly having three extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy at the same time he was mingling with President Donald Trump. That’s because Huang wasn’t merely running the first $5 trillion company, he was the visionary leader in control of the must-have GPUs powering the worldwide AI boom, part of a company that represents around 6 percent of the S&P 500 stock market index all by itself. The 63-year-old once said he preferred to die on the job; he once suggested he’d work until he was 90 or 100, then carry on leading the company as a robot. It’s not easy to replace Huang, partly because he had no deputies. Around 60 employees reported directly to the CEO. “He built the company around himself, and everything that happened there flowed through him,” says IDC analyst and former computing journalist Tom Mainelli. “Jensen is Nvidia, and Nvidia is Jensen,” Jon Peddie, a computer industry analyst who’s been tracking Nvidia since its inception, tells me. He has left the company he cofounded 33 years ago. It’s the end of an era, and not just for Nvidia — because Jensen Huang was Big Tech’s last true example of a visionary showman founder CEO. “He was both the visionary and the tactical leader, the closest thing tech has had to Steve Jobs,” Moor Insights & Strategy chief analyst Pat Moorhead tells me. Elon Musk didn’t exactly found Tesla and has quite the track record of broken promises, and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg has proven to be neither visionary nor showman so far. Google’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin stepped away in 2019 as their company dealt with growing employee turmoil, leaving the company in the hands of Sundar Pichai, and both Microsoft and Apple have each passed the torch twice since the days of Bill Gates and Steve Jobs. Some say Apple’s Steve Jobs broke the CEO mold, but he created a mold of his own. Huang was one of countless tech leaders who followed his example by introducing their products in keynote speeches, adopting a single recognizable piece of clothing like Jobs’ trademark black turtleneck, and even occasionally teasing “one more thing” for the surprise at the end of their presentations. I thought Huang might be a Jobs wannabe, too, the first time I saw that he’d adopted a black jacket as his uniform. (It was not always a leather jacket; an earlier version was a Nvidia-branded softshell.) Huang later insisted on wearing a jacket even when the temperature was hot — more than once, I saw him sweat profusely rather than take it off. Unlike Jobs, he also held quite a few keynotes when he didn’t have much news to share; he liked to repeat the company’s previous accomplishments as if they were brand-new. But even if Huang didn’t have the same gravitas as Jobs, he did have exciting tech up his sleeves and loved to demo it onstage. He took Nvidia to fame and fortune through a series of tremendous bets. In 1996, three years after he cofounded the company at a Denny’s diner, Nvidia nearly went out of business while working on a failed graphics chip for the Sega Dreamcast game console. But even though he didn’t deliver that chip, Huang personally convinced Sega to invest $5 million afterward, The Wall Street Journal reported in 2024. He then turned around and bet the company again on the Riva 128 PC graphics accelerator, an effort so ambitious he had to lay off over half of Nvidia’s roughly 100 staffers, skip the prototyping stage, and rush it straight to production, and he still only had one month of payroll left by the time it shipped, The New Yorker wrote in 2023. Thankfully, it was a success, selling a million units in just four months and paving the way for both the GeForce GPU and a long-term relationship with chip fabricator TSMC. Roughly eight years later, Huang decided it wasn’t enough to be the leader in PC gaming graphics alone. He bet the company’s entire gross profit, he told podcaster Lex Fridman, on shipping a new feature inside those graphics cards that no one had asked for: CUDA. It was the ability to use a GPU for other kinds of computing tasks beyond graphics, and Huang said it increased the cost of every GeForce graphics card by 50 percent. “Jensen had the vision for what it could be and the courage to pursue it in spite of the opinions of others.” “NVIDIA was effectively investing in a computing platform that extended far beyond graphics, with no guarantee of a near-term return,” says HotTech analyst Dave Altavilla. “Huang saw that a GPU was really a parallel computer that happened to render graphics. CUDA turned that insight into a platform, and it’s why NVIDIA was ready when AI arrived,” Mainelli tells me. When the Great Recession hit in 2007–2009, and Nvidia laptop graphics chips also started failing due to design defects, the company lost 80 percent of its market value. But Huang believed in CUDA enough to invest even more. “He literally handed out high-end NVIDIA GPUs to researchers at industry conferences, while the company seeded universities like Stanford with hardware to encourage development on its platform,” says Altavilla. And by 2012, Nvidia’s potential for AI had started to emerge. That’s when University of Toronto researchers used Nvidia GPUs to train a prize-winning image-recognition neural network called AlexNet, which is widely credited for sparking the AI revolution. Not all of Huang’s visions panned out the way he publicly expected. That AlexNet demo directly led to Huang’s bets on chips for self-driving cars, he said, but he didn’t exactly predict AI — CUDA was instead thought of as better and more affordable supercomputing for researchers and scientists.

sources.title: The Swift Downfall of Jensen Huang and What’s Next for Nvidia - New York Magazine
passages: Less than two weeks ago, billionaire Jensen Huang was a gainfully employed CEO whose personal life the general public knew very little about; today, he’s out at Nvidia, the multitrillion-dollar company he co-founded in 1993, following revelations that he had an affair with (1) a woman accused of being a Chinese spy and (2) an Nvidia subordinate.

The stunning downfall will undoubtedly have reverberations far beyond Nvidia’s Silicon Valley campus, given Huang’s position as one of the most powerful, if not the most powerful, figures in the AI industry and his close proximity to Donald Trump.
On Wall Street, the company’s stock was down 11 percent on the news of his departure, which translates to a loss of roughly $1 trillion just this month.

In Washington, the New York Times notes that few tech executives “have had as much sway as Huang over Trump’s approach to A.I. and China.” He reportedly “persuaded the president to roll back a ban on chip sales to China and Nvidia has donated at least $20 million to a fund for Trump’s White House ballroom project.”

On Wednesday Nvidia’s board met for hours to decide Huang’s fate, and, despite the CEO reportedly “fighting hard to hang onto his role with the company he founded,” Huang resigned Thursday morning and chief financial officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO.

Incredibly, Nvidia had no successor in place prior to the scandal that took down its leader because Huang didn’t believe in succession planning ; he was also apparently a micromanager with 60 direct reports and said last year that he reads thousands of employee emails a day.
I support the investigation and will cooperate fully.
I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security.
Q: When were you first informed that there was an issue with Jensen Huang and the affair and what was presented to you at the time?
I believe he is suffering greatly because of his family, his wife, who he loves, and his family.
During the conference, Nvidia executives were at a nearby hotel for meetings.
Powell were seen being affectionate at the hotel.
One bystander captured the interaction on their phone, three people briefed on the incident said.
The board also says it has appointed its first-ever chairman, Harvey Jones, the former CEO of Synopsys.

The Times reports that a “monthslong investigation” into Megaspeed, and whether it was “smuggling Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips into China,” was suddenly paused “after Commerce Department investigators working on the case received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel seeking information about the inquiry.” Agents were reportedly alarmed when Nvidia’s general counsel said that a top Commerce official who reports directly to Secretary Howard Lutnick “had given Nvidia permission to reach out about the case.”
Powell appeared at GTC, Nvidia’s annual developer conference in San Jose, where she spoke about using A.I. to aid in breakthroughs in health care and biology.
Her presentation used cartoon depictions of Mr.

Less than two weeks ago, billionaire Jensen Huang was a gainfully employed CEO whose personal life the general public knew very little about; today, he’s out at Nvidia, the multitrillion-dollar company he co-founded in 1993, following revelations that he had an affair with (1) a woman accused of being a Chinese spy and (2) an Nvidia subordinate. On Wednesday Nvidia’s board met for hours to decide Huang’s fate, and, despite the CEO reportedly “fighting hard to hang onto his role with the company he founded,” Huang resigned Thursday morning and chief financial officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO. Incredibly, Nvidia had no successor in place prior to the scandal that took down its leader because Huang didn’t believe in succession planning ; he was also apparently a micromanager with 60 direct reports and said last year that he reads thousands of employee emails a day. According to The Information, Huang told colleagues in the past several years that he would run Nvidia until he is 120 years old. Which is all well and good if you’re planning to both (a) live that long and (b) not have an affair with an accused Chinese spy. Otherwise it’s pretty risky! The stunning downfall will undoubtedly have reverberations far beyond Nvidia’s Silicon Valley campus, given Huang’s position as one of the most powerful, if not the most powerful, figures in the AI industry and his close proximity to Donald Trump. On Wall Street, the company’s stock was down 11 percent on the news of his departure, which translates to a loss of roughly $1 trillion just this month. In Washington, the New York Times notes that few tech executives “have had as much sway as Huang over Trump’s approach to A.I. and China.” He reportedly “persuaded the president to roll back a ban on chip sales to China and Nvidia has donated at least $20 million to a fund for Trump’s White House ballroom project.” On Thursday morning, Trump — who spent the prior days telling reporters how wonderful Huang is — recommended former Apple CEO Tim Cook for the job. Trump has gushed in the past about “Tim Apple,” who visited the White House last year bearing gifts . “A Legend replaces a Legend!” the president wrote . If you’re just catching up to the sex-spy-AI scandal, here’s everything that’s happened so far. In a bombshell story, the New York Times reports that after concluding that Alice Huang (no relation), the chief executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed, was a “Chinese intelligence asset,” U.S. intelligence officials made an even more startling discovery: that Huang “had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang.” The Times story also reveals that Donald Trump had been “briefed about the intelligence findings” a year ago and “chose not to do anything with the information.” In fairness, the president may have been preoccupied with ballroom renovations; at the time, he was fighting with his architect . In an interview with Bloomberg, the CEO insists his interactions with Ms. Huang were strictly professional. “Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual,” Huang says . He will regret this statement ! GOP representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford — who lead the House’s Committee on Foreign Affairs, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the Select Committee on Intelligence, respectively — send a letter to Huang telling him they want a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Ms. Huang. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” they write. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.” Democratic senator Chris Coons, who is expected to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee come January, writes on X: “The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I’m convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn’t corrupt. Congress will investigate and get answers.” In a letter to Nvidia employees, Huang — who denied the affair less than two weeks prior — writes : “I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” He continues: “Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.” In a statement, Nvidia’s board says it “has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.” Speaking to reporters the day Huang admitted to the affair, Trump says he would “certainly take” the CEO on an upcoming trip to China and that Huang “dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else.” (As a reminder, the president himself is an expert on affairs .) The president of the United States continues: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it … He’s done an amazing job for our country. You know, we have the hottest country anywhere in the world. We have the highest stock market.” Q: Is Jensen Huang coming with you on your trip to Asia? Trump: I’d certainly take him. I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong. He dealt with somebody but so does everybody else. pic.twitter.com/A2gKBTBEey The Times runs a story reporting that last year, the secretary of State “oversaw the drafting” of a “highly classified memo” that warned top officials in the Trump administration that Huang “was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.” The memo was reportedly sent to officials prior to a trip the president took to China in May; according to the Times , it’s unclear if the warning played a role in Huang initially not being invited to join Trump. (After Trump saw coverage about Huang not being included on the delegation, he wrote on social media that he was honored to have “the Great Jensen Huang” and other business executives “journeying to the Great Country of China where I will be asking President Xi, a Leader of extraordinary distinction, to ‘open up’ China so that these brilliant people can work their magic.” (Huang was picked up by Air Force One during a stop in Alaska .) In fact, he was told about it a year ago and chose not to do anything. Q: When were you first informed that there was an issue with Jensen Huang and the affair and what was presented to you at the time? Trump: I hope there is no problem. I believe he is suffering greatly because of his family, his wife, who he loves, and his family. But he's… pic.twitter.com/XtODQmCpre The Times reports that a “monthslong investigation” into Megaspeed, and whether it was “smuggling Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips into China,” was suddenly paused “after Commerce Department investigators working on the case received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel seeking information about the inquiry.” Agents were reportedly alarmed when Nvidia’s general counsel said that a top Commerce official who reports directly to Secretary Howard Lutnick “had given Nvidia permission to reach out about the case.” The board of directors announces it has hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to run the investigation into Huang’s affair and whether company secrets were divulged or national security was breached. The probe will be run by Joon Kim, the former acting U.S. Attorney for the Southern District who was appointed in 2021 to investigate allegations of sexual harassment against then-governor Andrew Cuomo. As it turns out, the Nvidia CEO wasn’t just having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, he was also cheating on his wife with a subordinate named Kimberly Powell, according to the New York Times . And apparently he’d been hoping to keep that affair on the down low. Per the Times : In March, Ms. Powell appeared at GTC, Nvidia’s annual developer conference in San Jose, where she spoke about using A.I. to aid in breakthroughs in health care and biology. Her presentation used cartoon depictions of Mr. Huang. During the conference, Nvidia executives were at a nearby hotel for meetings. Mr. Huang and Ms. Powell were seen being affectionate at the hotel. One bystander captured the interaction on their phone, three people briefed on the incident said. Mr. Huang’s security workers witnessed the bystander with the phone and sequestered the person, the people said. The workers then asked the person to sign a nondisclosure agreement. When asked by a reporter about the relationship by phone, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” and hung up. The Wall Street Journal reports that Nvidia’s board of directors “is preparing to oust” Huang. Of note, there is no successor in place . After meeting for hours on Wednesday, Nvidia announces early Thursday morning that Huang has resigned, despite reportedly “fighting hard to hang onto his role.” Chief finance officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO with the search for a permanent replacement starting immediately. The board also says it has appointed its first-ever chairman, Harvey Jones, the former CEO of Synopsys. extraction.body: The longest halt in flight departures to U.S. airports since 9/11 came after updates to a telecommunications system managed by contractor L3Harris Technologies , Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday, as hundreds of thousands of travelers were stranded by lingering disruptions. There was "zero evidence" that the problem was caused by something "nefarious" or anything related to artificial intelligence, Bryan Bedford, the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, said at a press conference with Duffy. The upgrades at "at least" one remote location were part of ongoing work of switching from a copper wire system to fiber, Duffy said. A router had "flooded" other routers in the air traffic control system with over 1,000 connection attempts roughly every five seconds, the secretary said, creating problems with airplane communications and radar feeds. The outage again thrust aging infrastructure that underpins U.S. air traffic control into the spotlight, along with the country's struggles to replace sections of it while operating the world's busiest airspace. "What we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3 Harris, or did they install a faulty router," he said. L3Harris said it is "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel." L3Harris said it has completed more than 70% of the switch from copper wiring to fiber-optic system. Duffy took the groundstop to seek billions more from lawmakers to modernize the system. Bedford said no FAA facilities went dark but that officials decided to ground flights because of "instability" in information feeds to air traffic control centers that handle en route aircraft at high altitudes and eventually to others closer to airports. "We were unwilling to take any risk that this propagation could actually result in a center losing connectivity with aircraft," said Bedford. He said officials weren't sure for about 45 minutes what was causing the instability. Flight disruptions continued on Saturday. Nearly 6,500 U.S. flights were canceled Saturday and more than 8,000 were delayed as of 9 p.m. ET, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. That's on top of more than 9,000 U.S. flight cancellations, about a third of the day's schedule, and more than 7,000 delays on Friday, though some disruptions were due to bad weather. Friday had the second-highest U.S. flight cancellations since a severe blizzard and below-freezing temperatures in January, according to aviation-data firm Cirium. Part of untangling from the ground stop includes getting aircraft where they need to be. The ground stop forced many planes to divert to other airports, while dozens of planes had to park with limited gate space because flights couldn't depart. Airlines run one of the lightest schedules on Saturday and are deploying as many spare planes and crews as possible to get travelers and employees where they need to be as they're eager to start fresh for the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday period. American Airlines , for example, is offering flight attendants extra pay to pick up trips, according to a person familiar with the airline's plans. Delta Air Lines offered crews double pay to pick up trips and gave them confirmed seats on flights to get them into position, according to internal company messages CNBC saw. United Airlines was also offering pilots and flight attendants extra pay to pick up flights through Sunday, according to people familiar with the matter. American, along with other airlines, said it would change customers' tickets at no fee or fare difference if the outage affected their plans and that it would cap some airfares. Around 3 million people were scheduled to fly on Saturday, according to Cirium. The FAA had halted departing U.S. flights around 4 p.m. ET on Friday, a ground stop that lasted more than four hours, the longest such pause on departing flights in 25 years. Duffy on Friday blamed outdated U.S. infrastructure for the problem and said Congress needs to approve more money to overhaul the country's air traffic control. Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have angered airline executives for years, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions. It was the second time the FAA has issued a nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks. Trump administration officials have repeatedly said it did not appear to be a cyberattack. "Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable," the FAA said late Friday. The disruption also upended travel for NBA, NHL and college teams , which struggled to reach their destinations in time for games this weekend. Duffy said college football teams traveling on charter flights could receive priority. "I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA to schedule their flight times and make sure they have games going off tomorrow," he said during a Friday press briefing. The Southeastern Conference announced on X that some games had been moved to Sunday due to the flight disruption. "We are in close communication with our member institutions to assess potential disruptions and coordinate appropriate responses," the SEC said in a statement shared on X. The National Football League said that it is putting in three backup referees for three games on Sunday because of the ground stop, "reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns." — CNBC's April Roach and Jessica Golden contributed to this article.

“Due to the ongoing ground stop, Air Canada has cancelled all flights to and from the United States for the remainder of the evening,” the airline said .

ET, @FAANews experienced telecommunications issues at facilities & TRACONs across the country - The FAA issued a ground stop was issued out of an abundance of caution while 3,500+ planes were in the air - Pilots and air traffic controllers followed established procedures to safely land the aircraft, bringing the number in the airspace down to under 400 as of 8pm ET - The FAA confirms they did not lose all radar or telecom, and exceptions were made to allow critical medevac, life-saving cargo, and law enforcement flights to continue operating."  In an alert at 4 p.m. ET, the FAA said, "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers. We will provide updates." In an alert when the ground stop was first issued, the FAA said all airports would halt flights "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety."  "All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice," the FAA continued. "Inbound international flights will be managed on a case-by-case basis." Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin said at the news conference that the public was never in danger through this process and that the ground stop was issued out of an "abundance of caution."  The FAA said earlier the ground stop was caused by a communications issue, but it has not ruled out a cyberattack. Friday’s announcement marks the second time such a measure has been ordered since the Sept. The most recent nationwide ground stop before Friday occurred Jan. 11, 2023, after a catastrophic failure of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) safety system, which resulted in thousands of delayed flights and hundreds of cancellations. Immediately after the initial alert, 3,100 flights were inbound to U.S. airports, according to flight tracking platform FlightRadar24. Departure boards at New York’s LaGuardia Airport offered a hopeful sign for some stranded travelers late Friday, with about 20 delayed flights showing gate assignments after the ground stop was lifted. Technical issues with an antiquated air traffic control system are nothing new. It’s never caused, or at least in recent years, not caused a nationwide ground stop, but that was kind of my initial instinct." A stranded passenger at New York’s LaGuardia Airport vowed to sleep there while another traveler faced a delay of several days. Fox News national correspondent Bryan Llenas spoke with passengers at LaGuardia on "Fox News Live," reporting more than 260 cancellations and 600 delays at the airport. Rosa, a Frontier Airlines passenger trying to reach Charlotte, North Carolina, said she had received little explanation about her delayed flight. "No, they did not give any other information, just to wait," she said. Asked what she would do if she couldn’t leave that night, she replied, "I’ll sleep here." Llenas also described speaking with two Canadian travelers whose flight to Toronto was canceled and rebooked for Tuesday. "That just gives you an idea of just already the domino effect we’re seeing as these delays and these cancellations start stacking up here," Llenas said. Duffy wrote on X earlier: "The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. We will provide immediate updates as we have them." That's their lane to talk about," Mullen said. I think that's what a lot of people are trying to make the comparison to, and that's not the case."  Mullin said all flights were accounted for, and there is no threat to the public. "We are able to communicate at certain levels, but, but it’s overwhelmed some of the systems we have," he explained. "Once again, Sean Duffy, Secretary Duffy, is on this. And they’re doing a phenomenal job in crisis mode."  Mullin reiterated that President Donald Trump had been briefed.  Trump later also told Fox News that it did not "seem" like a cyberattack, Fox News White House correspondent Peter Doocy reported.  The FAA told Fox News any claims there was a software outage issue are false.  Senior officials who spoke to Fox News Digital said the issue is not expected to be caused by "anything nefarious at this time" and they "don’t believe this a cyberattack issue." By 6 p.m. ET, the FAA said the ground stop was still in effect. "As en route facilities recover flights will be allowed to depart through coordination with the Air Traffic Control System Command Center." Several airports put out their own statements. Boston's Logan International Airport released a statement that read, "The FAA has issued a nationwide ground stop impacting flights at Boston Logan and airports across the country.

Previous ground stops came after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks and during a January 11, 2023, computer outage. The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop at U.S. airports Friday, November 13.
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy attributed the stoppage to a “communication issue.”
“FAA technicians are investigating the issue,” he said in a statement, noting that the problem affected all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.

The advisory issued to airports by the Air Traffic Control System Command Center said, “Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety, attention all aircraft operations, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center, all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice.”

About five hours later, the ground stop was lifted. Trump administration officials said something overloaded the old copper-based ATC systems, causing intermittent radar and communications issues. Although the issue appeared resolved, they weren’t confident it wouldn’t happen again and said it could take days or weeks for flight schedules to normalize.
It was the third-ever nationwide halt. Previous ground stops came after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks and during a January 11, 2023, computer outage.

The 2023 outage disabled the FAA’s NOTAM system, which provides safety information to flight crews. The agency paused domestic departures while it checked the integrity of flight and safety information.

An FAA investigation found that contractors accidentally deleted files while trying to synchronize the system’s main database with a backup. The agency said in its January 19, 2023, statement that it had found no evidence of a cyberattack or malicious intent.

extraction.body: The longest halt in flight departures to U.S. airports since 9/11 came after updates to a telecommunications system managed by contractor L3Harris Technologies , Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday, as hundreds of thousands of travelers were stranded by lingering disruptions. There was "zero evidence" that the problem was caused by something "nefarious" or anything related to artificial intelligence, Bryan Bedford, the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, said at a press conference with Duffy. The upgrades at "at least" one remote location were part of ongoing work of switching from a copper wire system to fiber, Duffy said. A router had "flooded" other routers in the air traffic control system with over 1,000 connection attempts roughly every five seconds, the secretary said, creating problems with airplane communications and radar feeds. The outage again thrust aging infrastructure that underpins U.S. air traffic control into the spotlight, along with the country's struggles to replace sections of it while operating the world's busiest airspace. "What we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3 Harris, or did they install a faulty router," he said. L3Harris said it is "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel." L3Harris said it has completed more than 70% of the switch from copper wiring to fiber-optic system. Duffy took the groundstop to seek billions more from lawmakers to modernize the system. Bedford said no FAA facilities went dark but that officials decided to ground flights because of "instability" in information feeds to air traffic control centers that handle en route aircraft at high altitudes and eventually to others closer to airports. "We were unwilling to take any risk that this propagation could actually result in a center losing connectivity with aircraft," said Bedford. He said officials weren't sure for about 45 minutes what was causing the instability. Flight disruptions continued on Saturday. Nearly 6,500 U.S. flights were canceled Saturday and more than 8,000 were delayed as of 9 p.m. ET, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. That's on top of more than 9,000 U.S. flight cancellations, about a third of the day's schedule, and more than 7,000 delays on Friday, though some disruptions were due to bad weather. Friday had the second-highest U.S. flight cancellations since a severe blizzard and below-freezing temperatures in January, according to aviation-data firm Cirium. Part of untangling from the ground stop includes getting aircraft where they need to be. The ground stop forced many planes to divert to other airports, while dozens of planes had to park with limited gate space because flights couldn't depart. Airlines run one of the lightest schedules on Saturday and are deploying as many spare planes and crews as possible to get travelers and employees where they need to be as they're eager to start fresh for the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday period. American Airlines , for example, is offering flight attendants extra pay to pick up trips, according to a person familiar with the airline's plans. Delta Air Lines offered crews double pay to pick up trips and gave them confirmed seats on flights to get them into position, according to internal company messages CNBC saw. United Airlines was also offering pilots and flight attendants extra pay to pick up flights through Sunday, according to people familiar with the matter. American, along with other airlines, said it would change customers' tickets at no fee or fare difference if the outage affected their plans and that it would cap some airfares. Around 3 million people were scheduled to fly on Saturday, according to Cirium. The FAA had halted departing U.S. flights around 4 p.m. ET on Friday, a ground stop that lasted more than four hours, the longest such pause on departing flights in 25 years. Duffy on Friday blamed outdated U.S. infrastructure for the problem and said Congress needs to approve more money to overhaul the country's air traffic control. Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have angered airline executives for years, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions. It was the second time the FAA has issued a nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks. Trump administration officials have repeatedly said it did not appear to be a cyberattack. "Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable," the FAA said late Friday. The disruption also upended travel for NBA, NHL and college teams , which struggled to reach their destinations in time for games this weekend. Duffy said college football teams traveling on charter flights could receive priority. "I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA to schedule their flight times and make sure they have games going off tomorrow," he said during a Friday press briefing. The Southeastern Conference announced on X that some games had been moved to Sunday due to the flight disruption. "We are in close communication with our member institutions to assess potential disruptions and coordinate appropriate responses," the SEC said in a statement shared on X. The National Football League said that it is putting in three backup referees for three games on Sunday because of the ground stop, "reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns." — CNBC's April Roach and Jessica Golden contributed to this article.

sources.title: Who is really footing the AI energy bill? Inside the debate about data center electricity costs - CNBC
passages: "In a constrained capacity market like PJM, prices have increased dramatically as data center demand has increased.
However, other markets enable a more fulsome direct cost allocation," Maeghan Rouch, partner at Bain & Company, told CNBC.

The companies racing to build the massive infrastructure needed for the artificial intelligence boom are facing growing backlash over electricity costs, as households and policymakers question whether data centers are driving up power bills.
Large technology companies have also worked to assuage concerns about their energy use, with pledges to cover the electricity costs for their projects or to develop alternative energy sources .
Hyperscalers should also clarify their plans to address rising electricity costs, he added.

Under the mechanism, consumers make payments for expected electricity costs two years in advance, ensuring sufficient power availability during peak demand periods, such as heatwaves or winter storms.

Such commitments could prove particularly important for "drawing support from communities that otherwise might oppose [data center] projects," according to Chris Howard, head of data centers account management at JLL, especially if data center development were accompanied by alternative investments in local communities, such as jobs or training.

However, a recent report from SemiAnalysis, a semiconductor research firm, argued that the expansion of data centers is only part of the story, and claimed that market design and policy decisions play a greater role in these energy price increases than AI infrastructure growth alone.

From rural Virginia to the Arizona desert, communities that once welcomed tech investment are now pushing back against data centers amid growing concerns that these facilities — built by so-called AI hyperscalers — are straining local power grids, raising costs for everyone else.

Retail electricity prices in the U.S. reflect the costs of generating, transmitting, and delivering power, along with other factors such as taxes and utility investments to upgrade aging infrastructure.

Under the mechanism, consumers make payments for expected electricity costs two years in advance, ensuring sufficient power availability during peak demand periods, such as heatwaves or winter storms. Future energy prices under the mechanism are forecasted prices based on anticipated future demand, calculated through simulations run on proprietary models and data. But with all prediction models, parameters may not always reflect real-world circumstances. SemiAnalysis argued that PJM's forecasts often overestimated future demand, particularly as many planned data centers in the area faced construction or assembly delays due to a chronic memory shortage. In the U.S., where regulations governing power grids are decentralized across states and utility providers, market design often determines how additional costs are passed on to households. Large technology companies have also worked to assuage concerns about their energy use, with pledges to cover the electricity costs for their projects or to develop alternative energy sources . Hyperscalers should also clarify their plans to address rising electricity costs, he added. "If they're quiet about it, that's going to allow the rumor mill to fly off the handle." Tech companies have also committed to meeting data center needs through renewable sources. Globally, these energy shortfalls could "create massive opportunities for energy producers, particularly when it comes to renewable energy," he added. However, skepticism toward renewable energy commitments within the U.S.' current administration has raised questions about how far such sustainability pledges will advance in the country, Howard said. Even so, analysts say it may be in the corporate interests of the AI hyperscalers to deliver on these pledges. "It would definitely be better PR," Einstein said. But public backlash could also prompt regulators to impose new rules on hyperscalers, Einstein added, "which is really not what they want." Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you.

extraction.body: Big Tech sees a culture war over progress. But the real fault line is electricity: drawing it from the grid and generating it onsite provoke different kinds of backlash, neither easily solved by public relations. This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid. One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport . Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out. Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand. The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid. But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out). The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale. Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency). Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do . But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation? Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that. But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something. So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin , where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia. But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.” Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape.
Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ.

It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words.

But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.

Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.

One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables).
The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport .

Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity.

The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company.

Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid.
But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out).

The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.

Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency).

Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do . But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation?

Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that.
But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something.

So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin , where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.

But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

You’re reading Dispatch Energy , a weekly newsletter on energy and climate policy featuring Alex Trembath, Philip Rossetti, Lynne Kiesling, Rory Johnston, and Roger Pielke Jr. To access more Dispatch reporting and analysis, become a member today. Welcome to Dispatch Energy ! Conventional wisdom holds that the Luddites, the 19 th -century English workers who smashed textile machinery to protest automation, were anti-technology. But historians of the movement have added considerable nuance: The Luddites were skilled craftsmen who opposed not the technology but what the technology did to their wages, working conditions, and livelihoods. This perspective lives on—opposition to technological innovation is usually far more complicated than pro- or anti-technology. What people care about are the real or perceived consequences of innovation. Luddite dynamics have been replayed in the context of almost every important technology of the last half-century: fracking, incandescent light bulbs, SUVs, childhood vaccines, water fluoridation, nuclear power, wind turbines, genetically modified crops—each became a proxy fight in which the combatants often let pro- or anti-technology symbolism crowd out consideration of risks and benefits. Data centers have now joined the list of contested technologies, and the fight follows a familiar script. One veteran organizer explained plainly why national environmental groups seized on the issue in an interview with Politico : “There is not a better way to be relevant that is as prevalent as data centers.” That organizer—Jane Kleeb, the Bold Alliance founder who spent two decades rallying communities against oil pipelines—explained the underlying strategy: “After doing this work for 20 years, it is easier to mobilize communities to block something than it is to build something.” I’m no defender of every technological innovation. But on the issue of data centers, the central question is not “Which side are you on?” Rather, it is whether the empirical claims for and against data centers stand up to scrutiny.
