extraction.body: The results of the U.S. midterm elections are in, with Democrats capturing control of both the federal Senate and House. Markets briefly fretted that cryptocurrency policy would shift toward tightening. But Matt Hougan, chief investment officer of crypto asset manager Bitwise (Bitwise Asset Management), believes the political shake-up will have limited long-term impact on crypto — and that any price pullback driven by it may instead be an opportunity to enter the market. In a post-election weekly memo, Hougan said plainly that what really matters for crypto is not the election but demographics. He noted that while Democrats made big gains — picking up at least seven Senate seats and a clear increase in House seats — the ratio of crypto-friendly to crypto-skeptical lawmakers in Congress has barely budged. According to ratings from crypto advocacy group Stand With Crypto, 51 members of the incoming Senate are classified as crypto supporters (rated A or B), roughly flat versus 52 in the previous Congress. In the House, supporters now number 241, a solid majority of the 435 seats. In other words, the party colors changed, but Congress's friendly foundation for crypto has not crumbled. Hougan specifically highlighted generational turnover among lawmakers. He described the wave of new blood as "the chamber turned blue, but the gray also faded": the average age of newly elected senators is about 14 years younger than those leaving, and the number of senators under 50 has nearly doubled from 8 to 15. In the House, Gen Z and Millennial lawmakers now number at least 94. He argues that younger generations are more receptive to the technology they grew up with, and that this structural force will eventually be reflected in the policy environment. He cited a Charles Schwab survey as evidence: 33% of Millennials hold cryptocurrency versus just 8% of Baby Boomers — a gap of more than four times. Hougan pointed to James Talarico, the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas, as an example. The 37-year-old Talarico, who takes office in January, will become the youngest U.S. senator. He holds an A rating from Stand With Crypto and voted twice during his service in the Texas state legislature in favor of establishing a state strategic Bitcoin reserve. Hougan casts him as a representative of a generation that has "coexisted with Bitcoin their entire careers," and argues that as digital-native generations gradually move into corporate and institutional leadership, the crypto policy environment will change over time. Still, Hougan is not overly optimistic about the near term. He expects Massachusetts Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, known for her anti-crypto stance, to likely take the helm of the powerful Senate Banking Committee, which can launch investigations into any sector when necessary. He judges that the Trump-linked meme coin "TRUMP" and World Liberty Financial could face large-scale, high-profile congressional investigations, and that sectors such as prediction markets will also bear regulatory risk. In Hougan's view, crypto markets could swing sharply over the coming weeks and even months as investors wait to see the Democrats' policy direction, but his long-term view is unchanged. In an interview on the podcast "Unchained," he said it remains unclear how Democrats will handle crypto issues, that caution is warranted in the coming weeks, but that conditions may improve before year-end. He believes the growth trajectory of mainstream areas — Bitcoin, stablecoins and asset tokenization — will not be much affected, concluding that "demographics determine destiny." extraction.body: The results of the U.S. midterm elections are in, with Democrats capturing control of both the federal Senate and House. Markets briefly fretted that cryptocurrency policy would shift toward tightening. But Matt Hougan, chief investment officer of crypto asset manager Bitwise (Bitwise Asset Management), believes the political shake-up will have limited long-term impact on crypto — and that any price pullback driven by it may instead be an opportunity to enter the market. In a post-election weekly memo, Hougan said plainly that what really matters for crypto is not the election but demographics. He noted that while Democrats made big gains — picking up at least seven Senate seats and a clear increase in House seats — the ratio of crypto-friendly to crypto-skeptical lawmakers in Congress has barely budged. According to ratings from crypto advocacy group Stand With Crypto, 51 members of the incoming Senate are classified as crypto supporters (rated A or B), roughly flat versus 52 in the previous Congress. In the House, supporters now number 241, a solid majority of the 435 seats. In other words, the party colors changed, but Congress's friendly foundation for crypto has not crumbled. Hougan specifically highlighted generational turnover among lawmakers. He described the wave of new blood as "the chamber turned blue, but the gray also faded": the average age of newly elected senators is about 14 years younger than those leaving, and the number of senators under 50 has nearly doubled from 8 to 15. In the House, Gen Z and Millennial lawmakers now number at least 94. He argues that younger generations are more receptive to the technology they grew up with, and that this structural force will eventually be reflected in the policy environment. He cited a Charles Schwab survey as evidence: 33% of Millennials hold cryptocurrency versus just 8% of Baby Boomers — a gap of more than four times. Hougan pointed to James Talarico, the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas, as an example. The 37-year-old Talarico, who takes office in January, will become the youngest U.S. senator. He holds an A rating from Stand With Crypto and voted twice during his service in the Texas state legislature in favor of establishing a state strategic Bitcoin reserve. Hougan casts him as a representative of a generation that has "coexisted with Bitcoin their entire careers," and argues that as digital-native generations gradually move into corporate and institutional leadership, the crypto policy environment will change over time. Still, Hougan is not overly optimistic about the near term. He expects Massachusetts Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, known for her anti-crypto stance, to likely take the helm of the powerful Senate Banking Committee, which can launch investigations into any sector when necessary. He judges that the Trump-linked meme coin "TRUMP" and World Liberty Financial could face large-scale, high-profile congressional investigations, and that sectors such as prediction markets will also bear regulatory risk. In Hougan's view, crypto markets could swing sharply over the coming weeks and even months as investors wait to see the Democrats' policy direction, but his long-term view is unchanged. In an interview on the podcast "Unchained," he said it remains unclear how Democrats will handle crypto issues, that caution is warranted in the coming weeks, but that conditions may improve before year-end. He believes the growth trajectory of mainstream areas — Bitcoin, stablecoins and asset tokenization — will not be much affected, concluding that "demographics determine destiny." Can the company that builds the machines to make chips outpace the company that designs the chips themselves? Here is how to choose between ASML (NASDAQ:ASML) and Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) for your portfolio.

ASML provides the critical lithography equipment used by every major chipmaker to etch tiny circuits onto silicon wafers. Nvidia is the leader in graphics processing units (GPUs) that have become the standard for training massive artificial intelligence models. These two giants are essential to the global tech ecosystem, making them top considerations for any investor.

ASML sells lithography machines that use light to print circuit patterns on wafers. It has a near-monopoly on Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) systems, which are necessary for the world's smallest and most powerful chips. These systems are incredibly complex, often requiring dozens of freight planes to transport a single machine and costing hundreds of millions of dollars each for high-end models.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $43.6 billion, representing growth of roughly 22.5% compared to the prior year. During this same period, the company generated net income of approximately $14.9 billion. Growth was driven by strong demand in both the logic and memory markets as global chipmakers ramped up production for artificial intelligence applications.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.2x, which compares total debt to the value of assets owned by stockholders. The current ratio was close to 1.3x, showing the company can cover its short-term bills with current assets. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow reached nearly $12.3 billion, a key metric for semiconductor stocks .

Nvidia provides GPUs and networking software that form the backbone of modern data centers. In its latest annual report, the company disclosed that two direct customers accounted for nearly 22% and 14% of total revenue. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, though its infrastructure is also used by major cloud providers and partners like Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT).

In the 12 months ended July 26, 2026, revenue reached nearly $303.0 billion, which was an increase of approximately 83.4% over the preceding year. Net income for this period was close to $192.9 billion. This massive revenue jump underscores how critical its chips have become for every sector trying to integrate generative AI and accelerated computing.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the company maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.1x, which compares total debt to shareholder equity. Its current ratio was roughly 3.9x, indicating it can easily cover its near-term obligations with assets expected to be converted to cash within a year. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 25, 2026, free cash flow reached nearly $96.7 billion.

ASML faces risks from international trade policies that limit its ability to export top-tier equipment to certain markets. The business is also sensitive to its customers' investment cycles, which may delay large equipment purchases during economic downturns. Furthermore, any disruption in the complex supply chain required to build its massive machines could stall production.

Nvidia faces significant risks from evolving U.S. and international export controls, which have effectively prevented the company from competing in certain data center markets. Intense competition exists from established rivals like Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) and large cloud service providers like Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) developing internal AI solutions. The company is also vulnerable to supply chain volatility and a high dependency on a limited number of foundries.
While both companies trade at identical price-to-sales multiples, Nvidia appears significantly cheaper on a forward earnings basis.

ASML is my pick for 2027 and a long holding period, because its risks are about timing, not about being displaced. A weak year for chip equipment orders hurts its results but doesn't threaten its place in the supply chain. ASML also gets paid regardless of which chip designer wins, since a challenger to Nvidia would still need its machines to make chips. A rival would have to replicate the machine and the years of engineering that went into it, and ASML has stayed ahead of that for a long time. I expect that to continue, though no business is completely safe. Nvidia is a harder call right now. There are too many "unknown unknowns" after Jensen Huang's resignation and pending investigations for me to add to my position. I may need to take a few quarters or a year to see how things shake out. I'll be watching who the board names as permanent CEO, how the investigations and lawsuit resolve, and how the next few earnings reports read. I feel no urgency to run toward that fire right now.

Jensen Huang has resigned as President and Chief Executive Officer at NVIDIA. Sean Sweeney has become CIO of the City of Charleston, South Carolina. extraction.body: The leading open-weight models developed by Chinese companies were trained on Nvidia chips that the U.S. government restricted from shipping to its largest geopolitical rival, a new research effort claims. The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Alice Huang has also been alleged to be an agent of China’s intelligence service. While Jensen Huang’s relationships with a customer and two employees have drawn the most public interest, Nvidia’s potential corporate liability for export control violations likely factored into its decision to part ways with Huang. U.S. export controls are intended to protect the country’s leadership in AI capabilities against China, but Huang has long sought to open up that market. Blackwell GPUs are banned from export to China or Chinese-owned firms, while the Trump administration allows Nvidia to export the H200, a less powerful chip, provided shipments take a circuitous shipping route that allows the U.S. to claim a 25% tariff. Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who leads the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs, analyzed the weights — the unique structure — of large language models released openly by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group. The weights still reflect the configurations of the chips used to train them, and DePue was able to find compelling evidence that the most closely watched models, including Moonshot’s Kimi’s K3 releases and DeepSeek’s V4 models, bear fingerprints from training on Blackwell chips. White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios said earlier this year that Moonshot had used export-banned Nvidia chips, citing U.S. intelligence sources. Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, estimates that about two million advanced chips entered China in 2024 and 2025 through schemes designed to hide their final destination. That doesn’t mean that these models were trained entirely on Nvidia chips, or that export control laws were necessarily violated; the chips could have been in an offshore data center, which has proven a popular way for Chinese firms to access compute and driven an industrial revolution in Malaysia. Epoch’s data estimates that 275,000 Nvidia AI accelerators were imported to Malaysia in 2024 and 2025. However, the ostensible goal of the export bans is to prevent exactly that: Chinese AI labs training on the most powerful chips. China hawks have long called for stronger controls on who uses chips, not just who owns them or where they are installed. “If we care about the U.S. tech edge, it doesn’t make any sense to me that you would not allow Chinese companies to access chips in mainland China or Hong Kong and Macau, but then say, actually, if you just go over to Malaysia, you can do whatever you want,” Sam Bresnick, a researcher at the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told TechCrunch this summer. Megaspeed, the company led by Alice Huang, has been at the center of that trade for several years through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, and has been the subject of investigations by both the U.S. and S i ngaporean government. Friday, Bloomberg also reported that a company with links to Alice Huang was involved in smuggling banned Nvidia chips to a data center in Shanghai. In May, the short-selling research firm Culper published a report arguing that Nvidia had a “ China problem ” because a significant share of its revenue was driven by Chinese demand, either through remote data centers or smuggling in violation of U.S. law. It detailed Megaspeed’s relationship with Nvidia and alleged that Alice Huang’s companies are backed by Chinese firms that are barred from accessing U.S. chips. Ironically, short-seller Culper’s bet against Nvidia wasn’t driven by the expectation of a U.S. government crackdown. Instead, it was focused on the Chinese government’s response to the bans, which was to recommit to its domestic chip industry. If China succeeds, billions of dollars in Chinese demand for Nvidia chips could dry up. Some 600,000 H200 chips are reportedly stockpiled in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment into China. While Chinese companies might want the chips, observers have no consensus on why they haven’t been cleared for import. Graham Webster, a research scholar at Stanford who focuses on U.S.-China technology policy, said he doesn’t buy the idea that holding the chips back would drive domestic production, since demand for chips is so large. Other theories for the hold-up include preparation for a potential trade deal that would involve importing a large volume of U.S. goods, or concerns about potential surveillance technology in the chips. For now, U.S. companies have limited obligations to track what their customers do with controlled goods like AI chips. However, Jensen Huang’s personal and professional entanglements with Alice Huang create a much bigger problem for Nvidia if government investigators confirm that chip smuggling took place and that he was aware of it. Nvidia and Huang have both vouched for Megaspeed’s data centers, saying Nvidia officials had visited them to confirm they were legitimate. The U.S. government’s treatment of Nvidia and Megaspeed is also under scrutiny. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, who oversees the agencies that license chip exports, could reportedly lose his job after reports that his investigators failed to uncover suspicious chip buyers and were too cozy with Nvidia officials. The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Alice Huang has also been alleged to be an agent of China’s intelligence service.

While Jensen Huang’s relationships with a customer and two employees have drawn the most public interest, Nvidia’s potential corporate liability for export control violations likely factored into its decision to part ways with Huang.

U.S. export controls are intended to protect the country’s leadership in AI capabilities against China, but Huang has long sought to open up that market. Blackwell GPUs are banned from export to China or Chinese-owned firms, while the Trump administration allows Nvidia to export the H200, a less powerful chip, provided shipments take a circuitous shipping route that allows the U.S. to claim a 25% tariff.

Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who leads the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs, analyzed the weights — the unique structure — of large language models released openly by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group. The weights still reflect the configurations of the chips used to train them, and DePue was able to find compelling evidence that the most closely watched models, including Moonshot’s Kimi’s K3 releases and DeepSeek’s V4 models, bear fingerprints from training on Blackwell chips.

White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios said earlier this year that Moonshot had used export-banned Nvidia chips, citing U.S. intelligence sources. Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, estimates that about two million advanced chips entered China in 2024 and 2025 through schemes designed to hide their final destination.

That doesn’t mean that these models were trained entirely on Nvidia chips, or that export control laws were necessarily violated; the chips could have been in an offshore data center, which has proven a popular way for Chinese firms to access compute and driven an industrial revolution in Malaysia. Epoch’s data estimates that 275,000 Nvidia AI accelerators were imported to Malaysia in 2024 and 2025.

However, the ostensible goal of the export bans is to prevent exactly that: Chinese AI labs training on the most powerful chips. China hawks have long called for stronger controls on who uses chips, not just who owns them or where they are installed.

“If we care about the U.S. tech edge, it doesn’t make any sense to me that you would not allow Chinese companies to access chips in mainland China or Hong Kong and Macau, but then say, actually, if you just go over to Malaysia, you can do whatever you want,” Sam Bresnick, a researcher at the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told TechCrunch this summer.

Megaspeed, the company led by Alice Huang, has been at the center of that trade for several years through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, and has been the subject of investigations by both the U.S. and S i ngaporean government. Friday, Bloomberg also reported that a company with links to Alice Huang was involved in smuggling banned Nvidia chips to a data center in Shanghai.

In May, the short-selling research firm Culper published a report arguing that Nvidia had a “ China problem ” because a significant share of its revenue was driven by Chinese demand, either through remote data centers or smuggling in violation of U.S. law. It detailed Megaspeed’s relationship with Nvidia and alleged that Alice Huang’s companies are backed by Chinese firms that are barred from accessing U.S. chips.

Ironically, short-seller Culper’s bet against Nvidia wasn’t driven by the expectation of a U.S. government crackdown. Instead, it was focused on the Chinese government’s response to the bans, which was to recommit to its domestic chip industry.

If China succeeds, billions of dollars in Chinese demand for Nvidia chips could dry up. Some 600,000 H200 chips are reportedly stockpiled in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment into China. While Chinese companies might want the chips, observers have no consensus on why they haven’t been cleared for import.

Graham Webster, a research scholar at Stanford who focuses on U.S.-China technology policy, said he doesn’t buy the idea that holding the chips back would drive domestic production, since demand for chips is so large. Other theories for the hold-up include preparation for a potential trade deal that would involve importing a large volume of U.S. goods, or concerns about potential surveillance technology in the chips.

For now, U.S. companies have limited obligations to track what their customers do with controlled goods like AI chips. However, Jensen Huang’s personal and professional entanglements with Alice Huang create a much bigger problem for Nvidia if government investigators confirm that chip smuggling took place and that he was aware of it. Nvidia and Huang have both vouched for Megaspeed’s data centers, saying Nvidia officials had visited them to confirm they were legitimate.

The U.S. government’s treatment of Nvidia and Megaspeed is also under scrutiny. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, who oversees the agencies that license chip exports, could reportedly lose his job after reports that his investigators failed to uncover suspicious chip buyers and were too cozy with Nvidia officials.

The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Alice Huang has also been alleged to be an agent of China’s intelligence service. While Jensen Huang’s relationships with a customer and two employees have drawn the most public interest, Nvidia’s potential corporate liability for export control violations likely factored into its decision to part ways with Huang. U.S. export controls are intended to protect the country’s leadership in AI capabilities against China, but Huang has long sought to open up that market. Blackwell GPUs are banned from export to China or Chinese-owned firms, while the Trump administration allows Nvidia to export the H200, a less powerful chip, provided shipments take a circuitous shipping route that allows the U.S. to claim a 25% tariff. Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who leads the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs, analyzed the weights — the unique structure — of large language models released openly by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group. The weights still reflect the configurations of the chips used to train them, and DePue was able to find compelling evidence that the most closely watched models, including Moonshot’s Kimi’s K3 releases and DeepSeek’s V4 models, bear fingerprints from training on Blackwell chips. White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios said earlier this year that Moonshot had used export-banned Nvidia chips, citing U.S. intelligence sources. Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, estimates that about two million advanced chips entered China in 2024 and 2025 through schemes designed to hide their final destination. That doesn’t mean that these models were trained entirely on Nvidia chips, or that export control laws were necessarily violated; the chips could have been in an offshore data center, which has proven a popular way for Chinese firms to access compute and driven an industrial revolution in Malaysia. Epoch’s data estimates that 275,000 Nvidia AI accelerators were imported to Malaysia in 2024 and 2025. However, the ostensible goal of the export bans is to prevent exactly that: Chinese AI labs training on the most powerful chips. China hawks have long called for stronger controls on who uses chips, not just who owns them or where they are installed. “If we care about the U.S. tech edge, it doesn’t make any sense to me that you would not allow Chinese companies to access chips in mainland China or Hong Kong and Macau, but then say, actually, if you just go over to Malaysia, you can do whatever you want,” Sam Bresnick, a researcher at the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told TechCrunch this summer. Megaspeed, the company led by Alice Huang, has been at the center of that trade for several years through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, and has been the subject of investigations by both the U.S. and S i ngaporean government. Friday, Bloomberg also reported that a company with links to Alice Huang was involved in smuggling banned Nvidia chips to a data center in Shanghai. In May, the short-selling research firm Culper published a report arguing that Nvidia had a “ China problem ” because a significant share of its revenue was driven by Chinese demand, either through remote data centers or smuggling in violation of U.S. law. It detailed Megaspeed’s relationship with Nvidia and alleged that Alice Huang’s companies are backed by Chinese firms that are barred from accessing U.S. chips. Ironically, short-seller Culper’s bet against Nvidia wasn’t driven by the expectation of a U.S. government crackdown. Instead, it was focused on the Chinese government’s response to the bans, which was to recommit to its domestic chip industry. If China succeeds, billions of dollars in Chinese demand for Nvidia chips could dry up. Some 600,000 H200 chips are reportedly stockpiled in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment into China. While Chinese companies might want the chips, observers have no consensus on why they haven’t been cleared for import. Graham Webster, a research scholar at Stanford who focuses on U.S.-China technology policy, said he doesn’t buy the idea that holding the chips back would drive domestic production, since demand for chips is so large. Other theories for the hold-up include preparation for a potential trade deal that would involve importing a large volume of U.S. goods, or concerns about potential surveillance technology in the chips. For now, U.S. companies have limited obligations to track what their customers do with controlled goods like AI chips. However, Jensen Huang’s personal and professional entanglements with Alice Huang create a much bigger problem for Nvidia if government investigators confirm that chip smuggling took place and that he was aware of it. Nvidia and Huang have both vouched for Megaspeed’s data centers, saying Nvidia officials had visited them to confirm they were legitimate. The U.S. government’s treatment of Nvidia and Megaspeed is also under scrutiny. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, who oversees the agencies that license chip exports, could reportedly lose his job after reports that his investigators failed to uncover suspicious chip buyers and were too cozy with Nvidia officials. extraction.body: Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees. At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago. Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew. Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions. Relationships between a CEO and his employees typically fall to HR, legal and the board, not security. But security specialists say any affair — even one inside the office — can give a foreign intelligence service leverage over an exec who wants it kept quiet. And Huang’s relationship with an executive at Megaspeed, a company under federal investigation, wasn’t an office matter at all. (Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.) Still, spotting the clues isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals. Some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times reported earlier this week . (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct . The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him, and Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security. Even if it had reached Nvidia’s security team, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, said a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said. Many companies also define security overly narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill , Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.” It would be surprising if Nvidia’s security team didn’t have a more expansive remit than most companies given its scale and business partners, but it’s possible. In fairness, some of it is simply beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone. What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he said. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.” The playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.” Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He said there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed. He said what’s newer compared with Soviet era spying is the relationships these services cultivate now often last years, not weeks. Technology can augment that human intelligence, Eftimiades said, pointing to IMSI catchers as one example. The devices mimic a cell tower so that nearby phones connect to them. A basic version can cost about $1,000 and fit in a suitcase, he said, though government-grade models cost far more, and there were a couple of cases involving Chinese espionage where these factored in last year. Eftimiades says no one knows yet if the devices were used against Huang, whose phone was presumably hardened such that compromises could be detected, if not stopped altogether. But what Nvidia’s security team knew, and whether it could have acted on it, will only become clearer as the board’s independent investigation and federal inquiries proceed. In the meantime, Eftimiades said he hopes the whole episode is “a wake-up call” for U.S. industry, which he said is mostly “clueless” about China’s tactics. “We have lost trillions [of dollars] in intellectual property,” is his guess. “Whatever we think we’re doing isn’t working.” Get an Early Peek at the Next TechCrunch Disrupt Disrupt, Startup Battlefield, and more will return next year, and you can be at the front of the line. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew.

Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions.

Relationships between a CEO and his employees typically fall to HR, legal and the board, not security. And Huang’s relationship with an executive at Megaspeed, a company under federal investigation, wasn’t an office matter at all. (Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.)

The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals.

It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said.

Many companies also define security overly narrowly, specialists say. It would be surprising if Nvidia’s security team didn’t have a more expansive remit than most companies given its scale and business partners, but it’s possible.

Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone.

He said what’s newer compared with Soviet era spying is the relationships these services cultivate now often last years, not weeks.
